Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in his capacity as de facto spokesman for the Canadian Wheat Board. In view of the difficulty of getting credit for those countries which are presently buying wheat from us under long term agreements, what action has the minister taken to ensure that for the next sales under these long term agreements these countries can get credit in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not the de facto spokesman for the Canadian Wheat Board. The Canadian Wheat Board is under the Minister of Finance, and I presume he is in a position to answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been in constant touch with the Canadian Wheat Board and with exporters on this very difficult subject. My understanding is that the sales for early delivery have now all been financed, albeit with some difficulty.
I am very much aware that there has been difficulty in this regard. As Minister of Finance I have felt that I should not give any greater preference in the demand for credit in Canada to people in eastern Europe than I should give to Canadians themselves.

October 6, 1966
Therefore I felt I could not intervene to give discriminatory treatment in favour of those people as against Canadians many of whom require money for financing their enterprises in Canada. However, I do hope it will be possible in the future to avoid as much difficulty as there has been in these recent transactions.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. First of all I apologize to the Minister of Finance for directing my question in the way I did. I only went on the news reports this last summer, and I thought the Minister of Trade and Commerce would now speak for the Canadian Wheat Board.
My supplementary question is this. Have the facilities of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, which still has an odd $100 million available to pay for insurance, been examined to see whether it would be possible to amend the regulations in such a way as to make sure that those countries which want to buy supplies of wheat at this moment or in the next few months can have access to this available credit of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, a very thorough examination had been made of all these facilities. As the hon. member knows, in our arrangements with the countries with which we have wheat contracts the undertaking of the federal government is to guarantee the repayment of the loans, not to provide the money. The Export Credits Insurance Corporation has facilities for extending loans for long term capital purposes, not for purposes of financing short term credits such as these wheat sales.
If it had been possible to use those facilities we would have given sympathetic consideration to it. In our judgment it would not have been suitable for this purpose. As I say, I am not at all unconscious of these difficulties, and the last thing I would want to see would be any prevention of sales to these countries pursuant to these contracts because of the non-availability of credit. This has not prevented the sale of wheat, and I do not think it will.

October 6, 1966

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, October 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Sharp for the second reading of Bill No. C-222, respecting banks and banking.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock yesterday I was addressing the house and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) with reference to the antiinflation drive that the government is now undertaking to fight a situation which exists not only in Canada but is world wide, with Canada caught in the midst of it.
I am not going to repeat what I said in the special debate on inflation, but this bill has a very significant meaning today vis-a-vis the present economic situation in Canada. In fact, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) yesterday stated that following the debate on inflation and the turn of events in the sphere of economics and inflation in this country, some of his outlooks with regard to the Bank Act revision had been somewhat modified as a result of his experiences and observations.
I was saying yesterday that according to the statement of the minister yesterday and his previous statements, wherein he had asked Canadian producers, particularly manufacturers and retailers, and the Canadian people as a whole to keep down prices and to tighten their belts for a little while, if we are able to keep wage demands under control we will be able to fight inflation. I should like to add one suggestion here. If the minister is going to tighten the belts of the wage earners as well as the belts of Canadian manufacturers and producers, he might as well get ready to start tightening the belts of some of our Canadian financiers also. You cannot hold both ends down, allow the middle to go up and thereby level out the economy. If production costs, wages and the cost of living are to be held down, you also have to hold down interest rates, the cost of which is necessarily reflected in the selling price of any product in this country as well as in the cost of producing goods.
This is where I do not follow the reasoning of the minister. He applies tight money policies across the country, in particular restricts loans to industries, and then says that we have to cut down on the boom or we will go bust. On the other hand, he asks Canadians

October 6, 1966
Bank Act
for greater production and tells them we do not produce enough. You just cannot make both arguments. No matter which way you look at his reasoning you cannot follow it. The minister thinks, hopes and suggests, but he does not give any clear definition of the situation or seem to know exactly where he is going.
I am reminded of a brochure which I had before me in my office this morning entitled: "A Fantastic Debt Wonderland". In the brochure there is a sentence which was used by Abraham Lincoln in 1858, and it reminds me of the position in which the Minister of Finance is today. The sentence reads:
If we could first know where we are and whither we are tending, we could better judge what to do, and how to do it.
That is about the best description one could find for the minister today.
I find it difficult to follow the reasoning of the statement he made some time ago in the special debate on inflation when I read his statement of yesterday. If we are to cut down on the cost of living, we will have to cut down on the cost of interest. I say that because when industry borrows money from a bank the selling price of the goods produced will reflect the cost of the interest incurred in borrowing the money to keep the industry rolling. That is a certain fact. This interest cost will also be found in the price finally paid by the consumer. After all, the Canadian consumer pays in the end for everything.
The minister has stated that in some respects the banks will have no ceiling on interest rates. This will leave the door open to speculators, and I think there is enough speculation in the financial field already. When we consider the activities of institutions which we call "near banks" and some of the finance companies, there is ample scope for speculation there without providing further opportunities.
In the statement of the minister yesterday the second proposal which he made, as reported at page 8354 of Hansard, was in these terms:
Agreements between banks on Interest rates both on loans and deposits will be prohibited.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, how does the minister expect to prevent this occurring? I often walk into public transportation vehicles such as buses and trains and see a big sign above the door saying: "Prohibited to spit on the floor". Yet if you look, Mr. Speaker, you will find spit. It may be against the law but no

one has been able to stop it. If there is going to be the same kind of prohibition in respect of the banks, we might just as well not put it in the law.
The ceiling on interest rates is now 6 per cent; yet the parliamentary secretary to the minister clearly stated in this house that the banks have found legal ways of getting around this. Why should there be legal ways of contravening the law when the law itself means justice? Perhaps the minister can give some explanation of this, Mr. Speaker.
I told the Chair yesterday that I was not going to speak long on this subject because this matter is going before a committee and I imagine that at that time the minister will have many questions to answer from different members of that committee; at least I hope so. I also hope that he will answer these questions to the satisfaction of all. There are a lot of question marks so far as this bill is concerned, and before it goes through many answers will have to be given.
If the bill keeps its present form, the only people who may be helped in the long run are the big financiers, no one else. The minister realizes that there are a few modifications which can be made.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Modifications might be made not only in the Bank Act but also in the work of the committee. One of the things to be looked into, as we are talking about the chartered banks, is the fact that the banks are operating with worn-out charters. I do not know of any other body that could continue its operation when its charter had expired. Three years passed by before the introduction of this bill, and I imagine it will be another six months before we complete our study of it. I am willing to concede that under the circumstances in the house the matter could not be dealt with more quickly, but the effect of such a delay on the banks or allied financial institutions ought to be a matter for consideration.
We ought not to have to wait ten years between revisions of the act, or between cross-examinations of members of the financial community, to find out what is wrong. The banking community may also have its grievances, but it is part of the financial machinery of the economy. We have the productive and the distributive sides of our economy, which are governed to some extent by the financial machinery. We ought not to wait ten years between reviews of the structure.
October 6, 1986

The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands said that this debate might widen the horizons and the outlook of hon. members. If that is the result, then debates such as this should be repeated more often. The members of the banking fraternity, that is, those who come from the chartered banks, the trust companies or from other financial institutions, ought to be available more often for cross-examination. We should not wait from 10 to 13 years before submitting them to such cross-examination and bringing in legislation such as this. This bill has approximately 126 pages and over 140 clauses. We are given this amount of material to discuss, swallow, digest and accept. It has taken 13 years to bring these matters before the house and if we do not do something about it it will take another 13 years before we look into them again.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we should bring representatives of the chartered banks and the trust companies and other members of the financial community of this country before the standing committee having to do with finance more often in order to crossexamine them. In that way we might be able to prevent these recessions and concessions. I also say "concessions" because if we look at what is going on across the border we see that we are giving quite a bit away to that country. The Minister of Finance will know what I am talking about.
That is one principle which should be established now while we are reviewing Bill C-122 so that the House of Commons may keep close control over what is going on in the financial field and so that this matter will not be left entirely to the Minister of Finance or to some of the big string-pullers. That would be an advance and something we could be proud of.
We worry about productivity. The only man who speaks in the house about financial matters is the minister. We have no way of reviewing anything that the financial community says. If the banks at the end of the year issue statements, how can we verify whether or not those statements are correct? We do not see the persons who prepare these reports; in fact, we do not see anybody. Am I to question you, sir? Am I to question the Minister of Finance? As it is, I would probably get more answers in this respect from you than from the Minister of Finance. It is not that the minister does not know but he will not talk.
Bank Act
The minister is not on the boards of directors of the trust companies or banks. He has to accept their statements. The minister says the law is there, but how is he to know if they are obeying the law or if they are speculating too much. I say that it is the committee's job to find out these things. That is why representatives of these institutions should be brought before the committee to be cross-examined. It might help some members of the house because it would maintain their interest in the financial field.
This bill, sir, does not allow very much latitude to the productive or manufacturing part of the economy. In fact, it does not mean too much to the Canadian people. It is said that there will not be an interest ceiling. Is one to question each bank in order to find out the maximum it will charge? Is one to go from bank to bank asking what each bank will charge? There is already too much speculation under the present law, even at the 6 per cent level. If the minister would listen for a minute, also the member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin), it might help.
I wish to talk about the victims of bankruptcies. It is found that such and such a manufacturer in such and such a district has had a line of credit running between $150,000 to $250,000 for the past ten years. That credit is used to its maximum in the months of February or March, which are the low points for sales during the year. The manufacturer will reimburse the bank in June or July when construction gets under way across the country.
Then he is told by the bank to make good his overdraft. He has to repay it in three days. How is one to do that when there was no notice? Possibly there was a gentleman's agreement between the banker and the head of the enterprise concerned. As it was, there was no alternative but to sell some goods. The manufacturer did not sell them in the province of Quebec. They were sold in New Brunswick at between half and a quarter of their proper price so as not to disturb the market immediately adjacent to the industry concerned. But there is one very peculiar fact. A quarter of a mile from the concern in question there was another company in the same line of business, the president of which was a director of one of the chartered banks. That concern did not have its credit cut off.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
This is something which I believe the Minister of Finance should look into. There is a conflict of interest and in too many cases it

October 6, 1966
Bank Act
is decided in favour of those who are inside the financial field, not outside it. This is more than a coincidence. The bank director was the president of a company, and that same bank was furnishing credit to the other company. On a day's notice credit to the other company was cut off. The man concerned was forced into bankruptcy but the other man is still operating. No wonder he did not want to sell the merchandise in his own immediate area; it was sold in New Brunswick. If we cannot follow up such things as this in the standing committee on finance we might as well approve any bill which comes before us and leave the field wide open to financial speculation. These people know when the moment is ripe; they can sense it.
One thing is missing from this bill. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands mentioned it yesterday. It is a fact that we still have not recognized that there is a need to distinguish between the production side of our economy and the consuming side.
Consumer credit should not bear interest charges. As to the production side, yes, because the cost should be included in what the consumer pays. If we were to begin financing municipalities, school boards and similar bodies from public sources at very low interest rates we would be helping those bodies and we would at the same time be helping ourselves by cutting down every year the interest payable on the public debt. We are paying this year more than $1 billion as interest on this debt. To whom are we paying this vast sum? I should like the minister to tell us. To whom do we owe this interest? He may say that we owe it to the financiers. Who are the financiers? We do not see them much but we certainly hear a lot about them. They are the people who are far too often driving from behind.
Fifty, 60 or 100 years ago the various levels of government did not have the same responsibility toward the economy as they do today. Today the national economy embraces far more than it did 100 years ago. The time has come to consider dividing the economy into two parts, consumer credit on one hand and productivity, or the production side, on the other.
There is one instrument which would regulate both sides. It is not production. It is the means of distribution. It involves the representation of Canadian production in terms of dollars and cents. Until we change our method of financing we shall continue to face the problems which have so often plagued us
[Mr. Langlois (M6gantic).l
in the past and which will not be solved in any significant way by putting patches on the trouble spots.
I think the minister should seriously consider this aspect of our affairs. I do not go as far as to say that ours is a dual economy but the economy can be divided into two sectors, one which produces and one which consumes. Everything that is produced in this country has to be consumed by somebody or there would be no point in producing it, and if the consumer does not have the necessary purchasing power he is unable to pay for goods and goods will not be produced.
I am bound to laugh at the minister when he suggests we cannot produce enough. Let the people have the means of purchasing what they need. Let the producers have the means to produce and give them the markets they require. Let this be done and, believe me, production will double in a year's time or a little longer.
It is not only Canada we must think of. In the last great war 30 million people were killed in six years. Today hunger kills 31 million people a year, more than in the six years of the last world war. What are we doing about it? I suggest we are sitting back and saying to ourselves: this is the normal course of events. Yet we regard war as something to be dreaded, and when we consider the possibility of war in the future everybody shakes. How can the government ignore the fact that 31 million people died of hunger last year alone?
Of the $1,500 billion earned across this globe, 85 per cent is earned in North America and Europe. The share of all the other countries is 15 per cent. Two thirds of the world is going to bed tonight hungry. These are facts which the minister seems to forget. There is a consumer demand which is not being satisfied. World distribution is not being carried out properly.
We can produce the goods. We saw this during the last world crisis. Foodstuffs were being destroyed though the people who needed them were facing starvation. Where is the justice? Everybody is worried about this matter. When are we going to start feeding the hungry? If we were to do this, perhaps we would get peace. Peace is something we have to work for, and until we are prepared to work for it by trying to feed the hungry we might as well forget about peace altogether and begin worrying about the protection of our kinfolk.
Ociober 6, 1966

Let us begin to apply basic economic, financial and fiscal policies in this country which are adapted to the needs of the Canadian people and, if necessary, expand those principles across national borders so as to bring about the distribution of Canadian products to consumers by making the means to purchase them available. Until the government introduces a measure designed to reach this goal I shall be opposed to bills such as the one now before us.
It is useless to bring down measures which ensure that the house will be confronted with the same problem every 10 or 15 years. It is useless to give certain individuals more liberty in their financial activities while at the same time restricting the freedom of individuals among the Canadian public. The minister must think about giving something to the Canadian people. He must give them hope. By financial and fiscal policies he must devise a means of distribution that will satisfy Canadians and be an example to the rest of the world.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in the debate on second reading of Bill C-222 I wish to say it is my intention to deal with the principle of the bill by delving a little into history and posing some questions, because banks and banking are tied in with our very way of life, with our economy, and all facets of our lives are in some way governed by our banking institutions.
When we examine the causes and effects related to our banking institutions we are also seeing the tools which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and the Bank of Canada have to regulate the banking business and financial community. One of the most powerful elements in the world of today is banking systems, and here let me say it is my view that the Canadian banking system is one of the best in the world. But I also wish to point out that I believe there are certain shortcomings in our banking system and I hope some of them will be corrected by this legislation. However, it is not going to be easy to persuade the minister, and many other people who have an axe to grind, that changes must be made for the public good. I do not think we will get all the changes we want, but certainly we in this party are going to ask many questions in order to find out how far we can go to correct the situation as we see it today.
Bank Act
The government's monetary and fiscal policies are based on the banking system, and in this regard I am reminded of the situation that existed before the last war when our unemployed were housed in camps. They were allowed 10 cents a day spending money and many people believed nothing could be done for them. But when the emergency of war arose, through government policy our banking system created millions and millions and millions of dollars for the war effort, and these people who were in what almost might be described as concentration camps were taken out of those camps and given jobs or were sent overseas.
We found we were able to look after their health and provide them with clothes. We gave them tanks, we gave them guns, we gave them U-boats, battleships and airplanes, and it did not cost them a cent. As a result we became prosperous. What was it that brought about the change? Surely it must be known to each and every one of us that it was the fiscal policy of the government, related to our banking system, that produced the change.
I give full marks to the government of that day for the manner in which it faced the tremendous inflationary pressures caused by the great expansion of our money supply by the banking system. It launched a strong drive to have people buy savings bonds, but people were not told the truth why savings bonds were being sold. They were being sold to take money out of circulation. They were not being sold to help fight the war because money was already in too great supply in relation to the amount of services and goods available.
The government then launched into the sale of war savings certificates which, as you will recall, Mr. Speaker, cost $5 each. They were another means to take money out of circulation and return it to the central coffers of the government in order that individuals would not spend it on goods and services that were in short supply.
Then the government reached further into individuals' pocketbooks and started selling war savings stamps at 25 cents each, again not to provide money for the war effort but for the sole purpose of taking money out of circulation. But after a while we reached the point where all these measures were effective no longer and compulsory saving was introduced. When this step was taken people started to understand the government's intention in selling bonds, saving certificates and war savings stamps.

October 8, 1968
Bank Act
But even that was not enough. We had to embark on rationing and price control. As a result of the great expansion in the money supply there was a corresponding rise in the national debt, and the only reason for the corresponding rise in the national debt was our banking system which had the sole right to create credit. But once the national debt rose it stayed at a high level and then became greater.
We ought to ask ourselves why our government and governments all over the world are in debt. Each country in the world is in debt, but to whom are they in debt? They may say, "Well, we are in debt to ourselves," but "ourselves" means mighty few people in the world. We are in debt to the financial institutions of the world. Through our banking system we have created a large number of financial parasites which should be eliminated at the first opportunity. We all know that these financial parasites exist. We know the pressures they can bring to bear on governments. We know those pressures are greater than governments can resist.
With this bank bill before us we in the Canadian House of Commons have a duty to the people of Canada and, in fact, to the people of the world, to give leadership by adjusting our finances and our financial institutions so that we can have complete consumption of the goods and services we produce. We should strive to place ourselves in the position, as suggested by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois), where we can help the underprivileged people of the world. We should seek to place ourselves in a position where never again will we see stacks of tomatoes higher than box cars piled up in fields and then sprayed with some sort of chemical so that people cannot buy them. This has happened in the Okanagan where fruit has been dumped into gullies and chemically treated to prevent its sale in order to keep prices up. What nonsense, with two-thirds of the people of the world, going to bed hungry. Why does th:s happen? It happens because we regard our financial system as a sacred cow and are afraid to amend the law and make it function so that the people of this world can partake of the things which they produce. It is time we called a halt to this. I ask all members of this house, when we are dealing with the Bank Act, to consider seriously where we are going and how we can best adjust our financial system to the needs of the country and the world.
[Mr. Leboe.l
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The banks of this country apparently have found ways of getting away from the 6 per cent ceiling. I am going to mention two ways in which this is done which have been brought to my attention. First of all, people are being asked to borrow more money than they actually want and to leave a certain amount of it in the bank as a deposit. This means that if they want $75,000 they are asked to borrow $100,000 and they pay interest on $100,000. But the bank then has $25,000 in an account and this extra money in the account allows it, under the reserve system, to create an additional amount of money which it can lend and on which it can collect interest.
There are ways and means by which the banks are getting around the 6 per cent ceiling. Undoubtedly this is what the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) was referring to yesterday when he spoke. The other day I had a report that an individual who was borrowing a large sum of money was asked to pay for the first time in his life a large service charge in connection with his loan. This is another way of getting around the 6 per cent interest ceiling. The banks call it a service charge. They got this terminology from the finance companies, and most banks have two or three finance companies attached to them. These are ways in which the banking system is operating not for the good of the general public.
I am glad to see that at last we are going to put the banking system into a position where the banks can make loans and take mortgages. This is one of the things we in this group have been complaining about over the years for the simple reason that people were forced to go outside the country to get this type of accommodation. What happened in the financial institutions outside of this country? By a very simple process they were able to take security in Canadian assets, create the money through their banking system and, with a stroke of the pen, collect the interest on that amount of money. Therefore they sapped the resources of the Canadian people through a deficiency in the banking system in Canada. I am glad this is going to be taken care of.
I am also glad that the inner reserves are going to be brought out in the open, although I think the actual effect is not going to be too great because the inner reserves have been known to the ministers of finance of this
October 6, 1966

country and surely, if we have any confidence in our ministers of finance, they have taken these things into account. Now that we are going to know what the inner reserves of the banks are I think we will be far better able to assess the potential of any individual bank or banker in increasing the money supply.
Surely one of the things that will result from additional mortgage money being made available by banks will be an increase in the money supply. This increase in the money supply, of course, will have to be closely watched by the Bank of Canada and ways and means will have to be used by the Bank of Canada to make certain it does not create additional inflationary pressures. The only thing I can see as a real hope is that the flow of money will be cut off from other sources when this increase is brought into being by the banking system and therefore within Canada we will have the banking system creating the credit. In that sense too I think we ought to be more conscious of how the shares of the present Canadian banks are distributed so far as Canadians and outsiders are concerned.
We have devised means in this world of causing a distribution of purchasing power, other than by preparing for and actually engaging in war, by what we call moon-shots and launchings into outer space. In this field a tremendous amount of money is being released in purchasing power for individuals. As we know, nobody buys one of these rockets which are sent up and which are costing the American people millions and millions of dollars. Nobody will buy one of them but the amount of money distributed in this way is still very substantial. I am glad we have devised a means other than war to aid in the distribution of goods and services.
In the last couple of weeks I have been travelling with parliamentarians from all over the Commonwealth. The one word that was on the lips of most of these parliamentarians from countries throughout the Commonwealth was "peace". I should like to ask hon. members what would happen if tomorrow the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) rose in his place and said: "We have peace in the world. We are laying off all armed forces personnel. We will cut off all defence costs. We are going to dispense with the whole business." I predict to the Minister of Finance that we would have a revolution in this country within 60 days. We are not prepared for this type of thing. The financial system of this country is not geared in such a
Bank Act
way that we could look after such a situation if it arose. Yet we talk about peace when we are not in a position because of our financial structure to take care of the situation if it arose tomorrow. What would we do with all the people in the armed forces, those in the defence agencies and those engaged in the distribution of these goods and services? We would find ourselves in a good deal of trouble. So when we are discussing the Bank Act let us seriously consider how we can change the banking system of our country so that if we were suddenly confronted with peace in the world and in Canada we would be able to cope with it, because we will need the financial technique to do so.
In closing I should like to pose another question. I put it in the form of a question because I am not an expert in finance. What is so secret about the devaluation of our dollar by the same percentage as the increase in our gross national product? Common sense would tell me we are going the wrong way. For every increase in the goods and services that are available in the country we are saying that our dollar should buy less.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I pose this as a question because I think we should have an answer. The only result of this policy at this time is the reduction of the purchasing power of the dollar for the individual on the street. We will, of course, increase the amount of loans that can be made but they will be made at a higher interest rate. Perhaps this will assist the gross national product, but the financier will move in again under the guise of some secret formula that has been invented and take advantage of the increase in lending power.
I agree with the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands who has said that there has to be some control on interest rates. Surely there is no reason for a great fluctuation in interest rates at any time. When we divide the dollar we reduce its purchasing power in spite of the fact we have a greater number of dollars. There is no reason in the world why we should increase interest rates.

Mr. Speaker, I was very heartened yesterday by the minister's statement regarding this bill because I detected what I felt to be an amenable attitude toward suggestion from all parts of this house as to how we can strengthen and improve this measure, making it more acceptable to Canadians. I was pleased to note the minister's recognition of the fact that he had perhaps placed an undue

October 6, 1966
Bank Act
emphasis on the efficacy of monetary policy and that we should give consideration to other measures.
Many problems arise in respect of the measure before us. The major suggestion is that this measure, by increasing interest rates, will improve the flow of money in Canada and remove some inequities that now exist. It has been suggested that we remove these inequities first by increasing the ceiling on interest rates which banks are permitted to charge and that eventually we adopt a formula to remove interest rate ceilings entirely.
While we agree that the rigid ceiling placed on bank interest rates does not mean much in view of what has been happening not only to our economy but to the economies of other countries as well we consider it would be a mistake to remove the ceiling unless assurance is given that thorough consideration will be given by the government to the adoption of some means of keeping interest rates from skyrocketing. The government must adopt some means to prevent this. At a later stage I propose to move an amendment to obtain that assurance and I hope the government will give it consideration.
All kinds of inequities result from the 6 per cent ceiling on the interest rate banks are allowed to charge and we know that this interferes with the proper flow of money between banks and financial institutions. We recognize it is becoming more difficult to control this situation by monetary policy because the unregulated sector of our economy is growing at a faster rate than the regulated sector.
Banks are more responsive to the controls used by the Bank of Canada. We in this house all know of the various methods resorted to by banks to circumvent the ceiling placed on interest rates. I use the word "circumvent" in the sense that they get around the ceiling forced upon them in order to preserve a competitive position. The maximum interest rate charged by banks is really no longer 6 per cent but in fact ranges from 6 per cent to 11J per cent. We do not think that banks or other financial institutions should be allowed to adopt this position. If an interest rate is set at a certain figure it should be accurate.
Those of us who have been members of the consumer credit committee have been fighting for the adoption of the principle of a true disclosure of interest rates. It is important that banks, as well as other institutions,
[Mr. Saltsman.I
should disclose true interest rates and other charges placed on loans instead of the various devices now being resorted to by these institutions. If we require that other financial institutions in Canada declare true interest rates in simple terms we must require this also of banks.
The situation in which banks find themselves vis-a-vis other financial institutions is somewhat inequitable and should be corrected. As unfair as this may be to banking institutions, in the sense that they are required to charge lower interest rates than other institutions, we may have to accept this situation in order to maintain some control over interest rates. I suggest it would be more proper to free bank interest rates and adopt some method of controlling interest rates charged by all financial institutions in Canada.
I am sure we have all noted the indications that point to higher interest rates. Let me quote from the Ottawa Journal of June 21 which states under the heading "High Interest Rates To Stay":
High interest rates are likely to prevail in the Canadian economy for the next ten years, according to a consulting economist from Missouri.
That economist is Mr. M. T. Welshans.
Let me quote from an article which appeared in the Toronto Telegram of August 26, written by Stephen Vitunski. He states:
If you're waiting for interest rates to go down, you may be in for a long wait.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The Globe and Mail of September 7 carried an article by Ronald Anderson in which these words were used:
The high interest rates-a response to a seemingly insatiable demand for capital in all countries -is likely to persist for some time.
These extracts from the press are merely a sampling of what I think is a general opinion that interest rates have nowhere to go but up. Certainly this will be the situation as long as the present conditions prevail, conditions of a great demand for capital that exists in the United States, to whose economy we seem to be very tightly tied. There is also evidence to indicate that the use of high interest rates, even where high interest rates are deplored but are used in an effort to dampen down demand and control inflation, is not having the desired effect. Apparently this system is not working.
There seems to be no evidence at this time that high interest rates are actually behaving
October 6, 1966

in the way they are supposed to behave in slowing down demand. One might say that demand might be higher if it were not for the level of interest rates at the present time. But even with the highest interest rates that I think Canada has seen for a long, long time there is no indication that they are slowing down inflation and there may be a possibility that they are actually fuelling inflation in the sense of contributing to the higher costs of many industries.
In this connection I would give an example, but I think this situation is probably prevalent in many industries where capital costs are more pertinent than labour costs. In an industry where capital is very extensively used, a rise in the interest rate would contribute far more to increased costs than would be the case with a rise in the cost of labour. I refer to a report entitled "Costs And Earnings of Selected Fishing Enterprises In The Atlantic Provinces." This report gives a cost breakdown on a number of ships. It indicates that wages in one instance represent 1.6 per cent of the costs and interest payments represent 4.3 per cent of the costs.
This may be very characteristic of capitalintensive industries and as such should warrant our consideration in doing everything we can to maintain interest rates at the lowest possible level. It is very difficult to see how removing the ceiling on the interest rate charged by banks would lower interest rates in Canada. It would certainly create a reallocation of money from one group to another but I cannot see how it would lower interest rates, and it might very well have the opposite effect unless we took positive steps to control interest rates throughout the whole economy. I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Star of July 6:
An increase in interest rates on bank deposits will, in turn, force trust and finance companies to increase the rates they pay on deposits. Otherwise. they will go out of business. The net effect will likely be not only high interest rates on bank loans but increased costs of other types of lending such as mortgages and consumer credit.
In short, I think there is a very decided danger of a price war breaking out if some ceilings are not imposed on the general economy. It will not be a price war for the benefit of the lender; it will be a price war for the purpose of attracting deposits and the costs will have to be passed on to the lender. Then we will run the risk of having interest rate levels far beyond what I would consider desirable in a country that has to expand and
Bank Act
needs to obtain money at the lowest price it can possibly get it for.
I think there has also been a tendency for our monetary policy to be less effective than it might have been, in the absence of over-all controls in respect of interest rates. In some circumstances where money has to be tightened in Canada I think there would be a fear that such tightening would send interest rates far too high, far higher than perhaps the authorities themselves would want them to go. To some extent this has reduced our willingness for and effectiveness in the use of such a policy.
I believe that if we had more positive and direct control over the level of interest rates the government and the Bank of Canada could more effectively use their monetary policies in finding solutions to the problems at any given time. It is disturbing to find that we do not have, or do not appear to have, at government level the same concern about the bad effects of high interest rates that is represented by the concern of our neighbours to the south in the United States. The Americans are very much concerned when the interest rate starts to rise. I am sure that concern is also felt in this country to some extent, but the sense of urgency about such a rise does not seem to be as apparent here. I think it is necessary for our governments to recognize the importance of maintaining as low an interest level in Canada as is consistent with obtaining sufficient funds for our development.
We have always tended to be an expensive money country. Certainly this applies in our relationship to the United States. Our money has probably been cheaper than European money but more expensive than American money. In a country that has to be concerned about industrial innovation, that has to be concerned about making its labour more productive by the use of more capital, it imposes a very serious limitation on the ability of the economy to accept this move unless definite efforts are made to keep the cost of money low for this purpose.
I would suggest that higher interest rates affect the consumer in a very bad way both as a borrower of money and as a user of goods and services within which are incorporated the higher costs of interest, because interest is certainly as much a component of any product or service as are labour or raw materials. We are concerned about the general rise in all other costs and we have to be equally concerned about the rising cost of interest in Canada. This interest is passed on

October 6, 1966
Bank Act
and is ultimately borne by the consumer. Higher interest rates in Canada raise the cost of public borrowing.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
There has been ample evidence for some time of the difficulties that all levels of the government have been having in selling their bonds and obtaining money for their financial needs. We had the unpopular issue of government of Canada bonds amounting to $500 million which was not selling well despite the fact it presented a most attractive deal. There was some concern that it would not be sold and that it would inhibit the floating of further bonds in the years to come or that future bonds might have to be floated at higher rates. I am advancing these arguments in favour of the necessity of maintaining as tight a control as possible over the level of interest rates in the hope of seeing that costs both in the private and in the public sector are held down as much as possible.
I was very interested in the remark concerning interest rates attributed to Harry Truman, a former president of the United States, reported in the September 9 edition of Time magazine of this year. He said:
We will bring on a precipitous deflation if we persist in high interest practices. The result could be a serious depression.
It is therefore vitally important that a government should not permit interest rates to rise because of a depression psychology which starts to develop when those rates reach a certain point. It is far better to try to keep them level as best one can than to run the risk of allowing them to go up too high and then fall off, bringing about undesirable results.
Furthermore, I think the government should recognize that if the ceiling is taken off the banks and if we permit the kind of competition we hope will take place among financial institutions within our economy, then great inequities will become evident. In spite of the best competition, certain problems will arise which the market cannot be expected to solve. Those of us who for a long time have tried to get the market to respond to social objectives have come to recognize the great difficulty in trying to get this finely tuned mechanism which operates on the basis of profit both to have a heart and to achieve the highest profit possible. It is the government that should have the heart and the concern for those people who are hurt because of what takes place in the market.
[Mr. Saltsman.)
The government must assure the house that it will take measures to correct the social distortions that occur in the market place as the result of the allocation of resources on the sole basis of profitability. There is no doubt that social capital will be required. The market cannot provide this, and it is the government which will have to do so. It will have to build schools, step up its programs and keep an eye on interest rates so that these programs do not become too expensive for the public sector.
Things like research are the responsibility of the government, and I am sure the minister is aware of the great regret that was expressed in this country when in his last budget he reduced the sum of money that would be made available to research. The government will have to make development funds available to help those industries in Canada which need encouragement and cannot find funds within the market system. Funds will also be necessary for regional development. We frequently find that when a tight money policy is adopted and interest rates start to go up, then the already disadvantaged areas, just as the disadvantaged group of people in our society, are the ones who are hurt the most. The government will have to recognize this and see that funds are made available for this kind of assistance.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, and also to make as many as possible of our institutions, apart from the chartered banks, responsive to national policies, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the following amendment, which is prepared in French and English. It reads as follows:
That Bill No. C-222 be not now read a second time, but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house that consideration be given to the introduction of legislation to include provision for placing the sole operation of clearing house facilities in the hands of the Bank of Canada and requiring that all financial institutions issuing demand liabilities, transferrable and short term banking claims requiring access to the cheque clearing system be defined as banks and brought under provision of this legislation: and further that the government give consideration to taking such steps as are necessary to give to the Bank of Canada the power to set maximum interest rates on both loans and deposits as it deems necessary in the general interest of the economy in the light of prevailing economic conditions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was particularly impressed with the minister's speech yesterday in which he tried to define the purpose of this legislation to amend the Bank Act. He said, and rightly so, that it is intended to increase the degree of competition and flexibility in our banking system so that it will best serve the changing requirements of the Canadian economy and the interests of all Canadians.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a fairly far-reaching shift in emphasis because up until about ten years ago the purpose of the Bank Act was really to provide security or protection to people who had deposited money in banks so as to ensure they would not lose it. That was the emphasis found in the act, as is quite customary in the agrarian type of economy that we have. So the very fact that the government has realized the need for a shift in emphasis toward making money available for industrial and commercial expansion is in itself a very important matter.
Among the many items in the bill, I think one of the most important is the proposal by the minister that agreements between banks on interest rates, both on loans and deposits, will be prohibited. There is a presumption in the minds of a great many Canadians that bank heads or bank presidents actually do get together and agree to set interest rates. This is not so. They do not get together at a committee meeting or as members of an association and say: "We are going to establish such and such an interest rate for such and such a risk". That does not occur.
However, what does happen-this again pertains to a point made by the minister-is that although the banking system and the staff employed by our chartered banks are really quite efficient and forward looking, both are hindered because of the existence of cross-directorships.
It is strange to think that a bank, which is wholly a business, appoints its board of directors not for what the members of the board know about banking but because they happen to be well established and well known people. What the banks are looking for is an aura of respectability.

October 6. 1966
Bank Act
There is nothing wrong with this provided that the bank itself can function. Unfortunately, what happens is that the directors of banks, not being involved in the banking business at all or not making their living from the banking business, are inclined to protect their good names by being very conservative in their approach toward financing. This is all very fine in an established and very stable economy but it is not suitable for an economy which is changing rapidly from day to day as is the case in Canada. As a result, Mr. Speaker, if the minister is going to be successful in his goal of making more money and credit available to industry and commerce in this nation, he will have to do a lot more than just limit to 20 per cent the number of directors of companies who may become directors of a bank.
I once talked to the president of a chartered bank who told me that he spent almost 90 per cent of his time trying to gain acceptance by the rest of the directors of his bank of policies which his staff had developed. He said that on top of that he was successful only about 10 per cent of the time. In other words, banking itself, which is obligated to provide credit and has a responsibility there, is hindered by its directorships.
Let us consider the state of affairs in the United States. In most of the directorships of industrial corporations in the United States 50 per cent or more of the directors are involved in the business of the company of which they are directors. In other words, you have vice presidents in charge of production, vice presidents in charge of advertising, vice presidents in charge of sales, and the president, and then there is a limited number of directors whose responsibility it is to look after the shareholders who are not involved directly in the company.
We must remember that if the members of a board of directors make their living from the business of the company they are going to be much more concerned about its welfare, whereas under the other system we wonder how the directors of some companies make their living. I know a number of directors of banks and other companies who do not seem to be involved in any business. They are almost professional directors. They do not make much money as directors, but being on the inside, knowing when shares are going to be issued, knowing that they can subscribe to shares without payment of more than 10 per cent of the value, and knowing that the shares will not be issued until they are sold,

they are able to make money in this way. They make a living by making the purchase of shares of banks and other institutions a worth-while project through reselling them on the market.
However, this does not necessarily gibe at all times with what the banks want to do and should do, which is to provide more credit, among other things. There are no agreements between bank heads to restrict interest rates. But it is done in other ways. For example, over a drink or lunch at the club it is done indirectly if one director of a bank, who is having lunch with another director of a bank, says: "There is John Smith over there and he will be stepping into your bank for a loan; but he is not a very good fellow and I would not touch him with a 10-foot pole", or words to that effect. This results in an agreement being made insidiously.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I doubt that anyone can point to a definite agreement or even to a potential agreement made between banks to set interest rates. Unless we can take steps to loosen the establishment of directorates and to allow people who know their business, who want to be in banking and who are interested in banking, to come in as directors of banks, we shall not see too much result in respect of what we want to accomplish, namely, more money available for industrial and commercial expansion.
There is some emphasis in the bill on this matter, and I am glad to see that there is at least some restriction with respect to the directorships of banks. It will be difficult for any government to try to make laws in this regard unless one can say that bank directors may not have an interest in any other business than banking. Another requirement could perhaps be, that at least 50 per cent of the directors of any bank must be involved in the banking business. In other words, they must be bankers. I think this may be one place where we will find difficulty.
Another thing that is not quite clear in the bill has to do with the fact that a bank may set any policy. It can be as liberal as it wishes in the granting of credit for business expansion. The bank does this through bank managers. It is both an unfortunate and fortunate thing that there is a curious pension plan in all banks. In most banks, when the manager retires he gets a pension approximately equivalent to 75 per cent of the average of his last three or four years' earnings. That is a very high pension. Consequently,
October 6, 1966

when a bank manager reaches the age of 50 or 52 and only has 10 years to go he does not want to take a chance. He does not want to lend money on even the slightest risk because he knows that he will be the one to be penalized in the event of a loans's failure.
Again, many people have come to the conclusion that whereas at one time usury was the charge made for risk, today it is the charge made for a waiting period which is without risk. Consequently, the banks are accused at times of wanting interest, without any element of risk attaching to a loan, merely for waiting until such time as payment becomes due.
These are things that have to be cleared up. We shall have to foresee problems relating to such things. We shall not see an immediate increase of available money for industrial and commercial expansion unless we can somehow solve the problems which will hinder the fluidity of money.
Before I conclude I wish to take issue with the last speaker and some others when they indicate they are worried about mortgages and about mortgage money coming from outside Canada. I am not the least bit worried about mortgages being taken by foreigners outside Canada. In fact, I think it is a good thing. There is a limited amount of money in Canada and that money can go either into equity or business investment or into mortgages. The only trouble with mortgage money is that it is tied up in bricks and mortar. Mortgages are worth less in real money at the end of 25 years, even when one takes into account the interest which has been earned, than the money originally lent. The money at the end of that time will be worth less than the original amount owing to constant inflationary pressures but this money could have been used to invest in industry, that is, in share or equity capital.
It has been the theme of debates for the last three or four years that Canadians want to own equity in their own industrial destiny. If that is so, why put more money into mortgages, because that money will be tied up? I would much sooner let United States citizens have all our mortgages. If they want to foreclose and take away the buildings, let them do so. Let us, however, induce Canadians to invest in equity growth shares and in the industrial and commercial development of this country. For that reason I am not worried about mortgages.
Bank Act
There is, of course, always the fact that interest has to be paid, but after all it is only interest. As the former minister said, we should not mind foreign investment as long as we need only pay interest for a definite term. In that light the emphasis on mortgages is nothing that we should really be concerned with. What we should be concerned about is making available for Canadians money for industrial and commercial expansion.
I am not too concerned about the power given to the banks to invest in mortgages. I do not think it will have much meaning. Mortgages are long-term investments and banks are usually not long-term lenders. They are short-term lenders. Though they will invest a certain percentage of their money in long-term investments, I do not think this will be a point to be concerned with.
I should like to go back to the original statement made by the minister, namely, that the purpose of this legislation is to make available more money for the industrial growth of Canada. I hope that after the bill has been considered in committee and questions have been directed to the witnesses and recommendations have been made, we will have a clearcut view of whether the banks will succeed in doing what is asked of them, that is, to do a good job in banking. When I speak about a good job being done in banking, I do not mean banking in any limited sense. I am not talking of banking controlled by an established elite which does not know anything about investing, is not interested in investing and is interested only stability. The picture up to now in banking has been one of stability. What we need is daring.
I hope that after the committee studies and examines this bill it will come back to the house and report on whether or not the banks are willing and able to comply with the demands of this nation. May I call it five o'clock?

The first is an amendment declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy or provisions of a bill. I do not think I need refer to the others. Indeed, this would appear to be the kind of amendment which might have been moved with relation to the bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act which was given second reading by the House on June 13 and sent to the standing committee. Citation 202(12) of Beauchesne reads:
An amendment proposing a direct negative, though it may be covered up by verbiage, is out of order.
I suggest that this amendment falls into that category because if the hon. member's objective is simply to defeat Bill C-222, that can be accomplished simply by voting against it when the question is put on second reading. Citation 202(14) of Beauchesne reads:
An amendment which would produce the same result as if the original motion were simply negatived is out of order.
I also want to say that although the words of the amendment do not include that the bill be hoisted for six months, it does have exactly that effect. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) referred to citation 203(5) which reads:
An amendment was ruled out because it raised a new question which could only be considered on a distinct motion after notice.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to citation 382 in Beauchesne which reads in part:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill-

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on the bill before the house, that is the revision of the Act respecting Banks and Banking.
On re-reading the speech delivered yesterday by the hon. Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp), we note on page 8354, left-hand column, paragraph (4):
(4) The present cash reserve requirement of 8 per cent of total Canadian deposits will be gradually replaced by a cash requirement of 12 per cent against demand deposits and 4 per cent against term and notice deposits (including personal savings deposits). On present figures this formula would result in an over-all cash requirement of 6.6 per cent.
This means, according to the new Bank Act, that the cash reserve requirement for chartered banks will be established at 6.6 per cent instead of 8 per cent of their deposit liabilities.
Mr. Speaker, let us figure out what this will mean. I would ask the Minister of Finance to pay attention to the following figures which I will quote, and tell me if that is not the concrete and true result his amendment will bring about.
Upon leafing through Canadian Statistics September 1966 issue, I read, on page 76, in Table 106 entitled Chartered Banks of Canada:
Canadian cash reserves-total reserves for chartered banks. $1,492 million.
Bank Act
And according to these same figures, this has made possible Canadian dollar deposits totalling $18,443 million which represents an average cash reserve of 8.1 per cent.
If we now establish an average cash reserve of 6.6 per cent-it must be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the total cash reserves will still remain at $1,492 million, which is the present amount. If an 8 per cent cash reserve of $1,492 million represents deposits totalling $18,443 million, this same $1,492 million cash reserve, which is at present in chartered banks, will make possible deposits totalling $22,600 million once the cash reserve requirement is brought down to an average 6.6 per cent, which represents an increase in deposits totalling $4,157 million. And where do the deposits come from? From the loans granted by the banks. In this connection, I wish to refer to a magazine published by the Royal Bank of Canada. I am not the one who says that, I am only quoting the Royal Bank pamphlet "Economic Trends and Problems", prepared by their Department of Economic Research, in June 1966, as a special issue for general distribution. On page 3, paragraph 2, we read the following:
Bank deposits increase when banks buy bonds or grant loans, because the people who sell bonds to the banks or obtain loans from them deposit the proceeds thereof in banks.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Therefore, deposits come from loans and by decreasing the average percentage of the bank reserves from 8 per cent to 6 per cent, chartered banks are automatically allowed to increase overnight their lending potential by $4,157 million without their having a single penny more, either in stock capital, claims or guarantees. Chartered banks, the very day after this bill is passed, will be able to make additional loans to the extent of $4,157 million, merely because the average percentage of their reserves has been decreased from 8 to 6 per cent. I doubt that the minister can deny what I am now saying.
If the Minister of Finance will listen to me for a minute, I shall ask him a question which he can answer when replying to questions in general. May I ask the Minister of Finance to listen carefully so that he might be able to answer the following question:
Is it not true that because the average percentage of the reserves will be lowered from 8 to 6.6 per cent, the banks, which will always keep the same reserves in Canadian money, that is $1,492 million, as reported in the latest issue of the Canadian statistical

In other words, chartered banks have just been granted an $8 million cash reserve.
Banks now have an extra $8 million in cash at their disposal, and an extra $8 million in current deposits. It banks previously had $80 million in cash at their disposal and $1 billion in deposits, they would then have $88 million in cash, (80 plus 8), and deposits totalling $1,008 million. What is done when it exceeds 8 per cent? This is what the following paragraph shows.
Banks may now dispose of $92 million more for loans, and their deposits will then increase by $92 million.
It is not said that banks have an extra $92 million; no, it is said that they have an extra $8 million in cash and because of this, they may, and I quote:

Therefore, this example goes to show that the purchase of bonds by the Bank of Canada for an amount totalling $8 million has caused an $8 million increase in bank funds, which has brought about a total increase of $100 million in bank deposits and, consequently, money supply.
Mr. Speaker, this information is given by a chartered bank. The Bank of Canada, in one of its monthly letters, admits that when it issues $8 million, in cash, chartered banks hasten to convert this into $100 million. They can do that. They have the $8 million and, all of a sudden, they are in a position to lend $100 million while having only $8 million. How much profit do they make? They have only $8 million, but by lending $7 million at the present rate of interest, which is 6 per cent, they lend $100 million. This nets them $6 million in interest; but they only have $8 million. Therefore, in the final analysis, they make 75 per cent profit on what they have, since they only have $8 million.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) finds that it is not enough for the banks to make 75 per cent profit on their assets. According to him that is not enough, so he will authorize them to raise the annual rate of interest on loans to 7 per cent; next there will be no ceiling on their rates of interest and, finally, by increasing their rates to 9 or 10 per cent on household commodity loans, banks can make as much as 135 or 140 per cent profit on their assets.
[Mr. Gregoire.I
Mr. Speaker, to hold a bank charter is to operate the most lucrative business; yet, the Minister of Finance finds it is not enough. He will extend the banks privileges so that, as I said a moment ago, they can boost their annual profit to $476 million, without hiring one single extra employee, even without building one single extra building; overnight, that is as soon as this bill becomes law, the banks will be able to make an additional profit of $476 million annually-I think that the Minister of Finance is giving them a wonderful gift, and, in any event, at the expense of the people, as my friend, the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latu-lippe) has just said. And who will pay for all that? That will go into the production costs and the costs will increase even more. And the minister is complaining about inflation.
Mr. Speaker, the minister should not complain because the man mainly responsible for inflation in Canada is the Minister of Finance himself; as a matter of fact, the inflation which prevails at the present time is due to tax increases. In the last three or four years, we have seen the federal government, the provincial governments, the school boards increase taxes more and more, and prices go up; the workers who want at least to keep up with the cost of living are asking for salary increases and the minister talks of inflation. But the man mainly responsible is the Minister of Finance with his continuous tax increases at the federal, provincial, municipal and schoolboard levels in the last three or four years. And with that new increase in production costs due to increased interest rates, a real period of inflation is in the offing.
The government itself will suffer the consequences because that increase in interest rates will be reflected in the first budget after the act goes into force, by an increase of $180 million in the service of the national debt.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance is doing a great disservice to his country. He is betraying his country for the benefit of the banks and the few millionaires who have always made profits from dealing in money. The Minister of Finance should instead create another system; in fact, he should read that little booklet, which has only two pages and a two-page table, and then say to himself that what the chartered banks are doing, the Bank of Canada will do it too. Then the minister or the government would only have to do exactly what the chartered banks are
October 6, 1966

doing, namely keep the cash reserves and multiply them by 12 or 15, as it used to be done or will be done under the new act. Then the government would no longer have to keep borrowing from the banks; it would not have to pay so much interest on the national debt; it could develop the country's economy, not by reducing the value of money but by maintaining its real value and the country would experience true prosperity instead of alternating between periods of recession and inflation.
It seems, Mr. Speaker, that the governments are unable to keep us in a happy medium, between the two; when they do not cause a recession, they bring about inflation. We jump from the frying pan into the fire. Periods of recession are always worse after periods of inflation because the money never reverts to the same level, it continues to depreciate. We alternate between the two as if it were impossible to find a happy medium, a period of prosperity without recession or inflation.
Mr. Speaker, for the reasons that I have just set forth and because I believe that this amendment to the bank act is the biggest banking and monetary hoax ever seen, I do not need to tell you that I am completely against the motion for second reading of this bill and I suggest that it should be referred back to experts for drafting with the Canadian people in mind instead of the bankers.

Mr. Speaker, other members of our party have dealt with the amendment that we proposed as being necessary to make this piece of legislation more effective and, as we all know, the amendment was ruled out of order. However, we are still of the same opinion. I will not deal with the arguments advanced by the previous speakers but I do want to mention another aspect of this question. I might mention to the minister that I will follow a more or less philosophical vein in my approach to this matter.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, everyone knows that the program of our party is based on our belief in the need for a mixed economy at this time in history. Of course, one can give different interpretations to those words. We believe that under the present circumstances we can best maintain freedom and

work for security and equality so far as possible by the introduction of a program which provides for public ownership in certain fields, for co-operative ownership and for private ownership, all carried out as the result of government planning at all levels in participation with the people or with local groups. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, our group maintains that this measure will not be completely satisfactory or effective unless it is amended along the lines we propose.
I understand that other speakers in our group will bring forward various proposals when the bill reaches the committee stage, and I am sure the minister will listen to them. However, I also maintain that this measure affects only one aspect of banking. This measure will never be satisfactory unless it is coupled with the Bank of Canada Act and designed to serve the credit needs of all the levels of government in Canada. This measure would serve the immediate and short-term requirements of the private sector of the economy.
I should like to draw the minister's attention to the following. I have always been interested in the attitude of the Liberal party toward banking throughout our history. Not long ago I read that when Gladstone was prime minister of Great Britain he made a very interesting speech in which he recognized that the banking fraternity of Great Britain was more powerful at that time than the government. I commend that to the minister's attention. I understand that was the first time in the history of the Liberal party that a prime minister of a country like Great Britain recognized the strength of the banking fraternity compared to the government.
I remember quite well that the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King indicated that those who had control over the banking institutions of the country, those who issue currency and credit, have control over the economy. He recognized that. Quite recently I was looking at Hansard at the time the Bank of Canada was first formed. I should like to refer to the late Hon. Ian Mackenzie. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that the minister might be interested to know that at the time I was vice president of the British Columbia Liberal Association Hon. Ian Mackenzie and the late Gerry McGeer were sponsors of a resolution at a provincial party convention in British Columbia in which they urged the nationalization of the banks of Canada.
