subtopic: SEAFARERS' INTERNATIONAL UNION-COMMUNICATIONS BETWEEN MARITIME TRUSTEES AND DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought that with that question the motion was going to pass without any discussion, which of course is the way the government always likes to operate things. I will refrain from reading the motion again because you have just done so, but may I at the outset say that it is not my usual course to expose to the glare of publicity the private or inner affairs of any organization. The internal operation and functioning of a voluntary, private group of people such as those embraced by trade unions should be the affair of that organization alone. To drag out into the glaring light of publicity such affairs, with all the misinterpretations that can flow from such action, is a course to which I do not normally subscribe. However, in this situation the circumstances of history are peculiar and I think necessitate a more formal and public disclosure of some of the activities of the Seafarers' International Union than would otherwise be the case.
The public first became involved through government action in this matter when the government headed by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) appointed Mr. Justice Norris as a royal commissioner to inquire into certain matters in which the Seafarers' International Union were involved. The hearings of that commission ranged over a long period of time, and some people make the direct accusation that partly because of the responsibility of the commissioner himself and partly because of his bias and prejudice the hearings resulted in the blackening and defaming not only of the organization itself but of a number of individuals within it whether or not there was justification for this sort of defamation. In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, and in addition to the royal commission of inquiry and all of the publicity attached thereto, certain members of parliament, some of whom do not sit too far away
October 6, 1966

Motions for Papers
from me, seem to have delighted themselves in harassing both the union and the individuals within it, or individuals who used to be within it, which again is a sort of public involvement in the affairs of an organization of individuals.
Parliament also became involved in the operations of the Seafarers' International Union and other unions when it passed a law establishing a trusteeship to take over and conduct the affairs of certain unions, a trusteeship, incidentally, which I understand expires at the end of this year unless the government takes action to keep it in existence.
It might be well to note that our position on this question is shown by a bill which I have on the order paper seeking to repeal the maritime trusteeship act immediately without waiting for its normal death at the end of this year. By repealing this act we will thus remove the possibility that the government, as a result of pressure from sources unknown, may seek to extend the term of office of the trustees.
Because of the publicity attached to the operations of the Seafarers' International Union there have arisen a number of false accusations, smears and innuendos on the part of individuals with particular axes to grind, either because they have become upset at not having won election within the Seafarers' International Union or for some other reason. These people have solicited the aid of members of parliament who have used the floor of this House of Commons to carry out a persistent attack.
This attack, which has been diminishing in recent months, has caused so much concern to the union itself-as I say, most of these accusations are false and are innuendos made for particular and narrow purposes-that it has had a deleterious effect upon the employees of shipping companies as well as a damaging effect upon the well-being, the welfare, the wages, hours and working conditions of sailors. This is because the organization to which they belong has been hampered and harassed by the spate of accusations which have poured forth as a result of public and government involvement in this one private organization. There is no question, Mr. Speaker, that certain ship owners rub their hands with glee at such a situation, and I am told they have been responsible in part for financing the continued tirade against this particular group.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I am not one of those who believe in delving into the private affairs of organizations but things have got to the point where I think it is necessary to bring out into public light, as the motion requests, any communications exchanged between the maritime trustees, the group established by this parliament to be responsible for administering the affairs of certain unions operating on the seaway and in waterfront areas, or any other organizations and persons, and the Minister of Labour or any official of the Department of Labour, with respect to the Seafarers' International Union so they can be exposed now to public scrutiny. In this way we can discover, if it is possible to discover, whether in the opinion of the maritime trustees there was any wrongdoing on the part of individuals. If there was wrongdoing on the part of individuals, then the responsibility devolves on the Minister of Justice to take corrective action, to engage in any necessary litigation in order to punish those who may have been involved in wrongdoing, and also to see that those whose names have been smeared from one end of the country to the other are cleared by the exposing of information which the maritime trustees have had at their disposal. They have been the administrators of the union.
The purpose of the motion is to seek to make public these documents purely for the purpose of clearing those who are innocent and, if there are any who are guilty, to disclose the extent of their guilt so that all can see what has occurred. In that way one can insist that the government take the necessary corrective action to deal with those individuals if they have done anything contrary to the Criminal Code which requires prosecution.

speechtext:
I never thought there was another minister of external affairs in the house. I now know that there is another hon. member with the same qualifications.
First, I want to deal with the report of Mr. Justice Norris, who was an independent commissioner. Nowhere has it been suggested, even if he had political affiliations, as some judges have, that he had any affiliation with the S.I.U. I am certain that whatever finding he made about Hal Banks, the past president of the S.I.U., and about any other president of the S.I.U., such finding was not made because he was a Liberal, a Conservative or because he belonged to some other party.
After hearing the witnesses, reviewing the evidence before the commission and reading the documents, Mr. Justice Norris came to the conclusion-I do not have the report with me at the moment though I have read it on several occasions-that Hal Banks-and there is some proof of this fact because he had been convicted in the criminal courts of this country-had a criminal record as long as my

arm and that he had come to this country under very unusual circumstances. I do not mind putting those on record. I think the Minister of Transport knows something of this.
Hal Banks was brought in because the government of the day wanted to kill the Communist movement in the unions in Canada. So they brought in a man who had a criminal record as long as my arm. In reviewing the activities of the union one finds that Hal Banks while he was president, and in spite of his unusual investment of union funds, accomplished certain things. I will not use the privilege of immunity in the House of Commons in order to slander anybody. I will not go into details. My hon. friend from Skeena and others in the House of Commons Commons know what these unusual things were.
The judge described Banks in certain terms. He described him as a criminal, a barbarian and a hooligan who would stop at nothing for his own ends and who used the union for his own advantage.
I am one of those who believe that the unions of this country certainly deserve better leadership. They have a serious responsibility to the workers and they deserve better leadership than Banks or Hoffa or others like them gave. The documents in question might show that to be so. It was recommended in the report that Hal Banks be prosecuted for certain offences. That report was laid before this house shortly before our defeat as a government.
When the new government came in, because of pressure and probing from this side of the house Hal Banks was finally prosecuted. He was found guilty by a court of this country. He then filed an appeal. He got out on bail under very unusual circumstances and escaped to the United States. It turns out that the offence for which he was convicted is one of those to which extradition does not apply.
In this session of parliament, and I am not talking about the past few days since the adjournment but about the session from the beginning, I have continually asked the Minister of Justice why, when there is evidence that Hal Banks is guilty of a crime, he is not charged with that particular crime. I have asked why he is not charged and brought back to Canada by extradition proceedings.
The present Minister of Justice, the past minister of justice and the minister of justice
October 6, 1966

before that have argued or suggested, especially the present Minister of Justice, that they cannot get the documents from the files of the Supreme Court of Canada. We are talking about documents that should be produced having to do with the trustees and the officers of the S.I.U. The minister says that they are having difficulty.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
What I suggest is happening now is that because of the atmosphere surrounding the Hal Banks investigation the Liberal party- there is certainly some atmosphere in this regard because of the manner in which Banks was brought into the country and the questions which were left off his application, giving him the right to come into this country-does not want him back. So the Minister of Justice is hiding under a cloak. He says he cannot get the documents from the Supreme Court of Canada. Why does he not lay charges, bring Banks back into the country and proceed with the appeal, if it has not already lapsed, so that Banks can start serving the five years which I believe he was given for the offence of which he was convicted? He is one of the few Canadians who has been found by a high court judge to be a hooligan, a barbarian, to have committed fraud against a union, and then to have been given bail, allowed to escape and remain in the United States.

Nor do I think the hon. member is revealing any secrets when he suggests that Banks was brought into this country in the mid-fifties with the collusion of the government and the labour movement, including Mr. Jodoin and others, for a specific purpose, to clean up a rather unsavoury situation that existed at that time. I am sure the hon. member remembers another occasion when he and I discussed the same issue during the debate on the estimates of the Department of Justice earlier this year, when the former minister of justice, the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), participated in that debate very constructively and objectively.
I asked the question why, since Mr. Banks' crimes were public knowledge, particularly in shipping and union circles, as a result of the courageous declarations of Captain Walsh and other people, the minister of justice between 1959 and 1962 did not bring Banks before a court of law. As a matter of fact, the Norris commission was set up by the minister of labour in the Conservative government two months after the general election in 1962.
I am not questioning the motives of the then minister as to why he waited so long, because I have the highest regard for the present hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr). The former minister of justice, the hon. member for Kamloops, admitted quite frankly, that it is one thing to know of the escapades of Hal Banks and another one to prosecute him with any degree of certainty that the prosecution would be successful.
As recorded at page 11407 of Hansard for February 17, 1965, the former member for Carleton asked a series of questions about reports on the conduct of Hal Banks. His first question was:
Did the department of Justice, in 1958-
The date is significant.
-through the R.C.M.P., conduct an investigation to determine if Hal Banks had been employing Intimidation and violence in the furtherance of union activities?

investigation-

I have heard it on political platforms and I have heard it previously in this house, and it is no answer to the question of why a charge was not laid by the previous minister of justice at that time. This was the rule of the hooligan, but as soon as the commission was set up witnesses volunteered to come forward because they could have the kind of protection that would allow them to tell the truth, the truth which finally convicted this man and forced him to flee to the United States. The hon. member for Skeena has shown partiality with regard to the affairs of the S.I.U., and I commend him for it. The S.I.U. plays a big part in the labour movement and it does not have to hang its head in shame. It is doing an excellent job at the moment. In co-operation with the trustees it has restored peace on the waterfront. I hope the day is not too far away when the S.I.U. will be free of the shackles of the trusteeship. That is not my decision to make. It will have to be made in the light of the report of the trustees who may make that recommendation at the end of this year. That is incidental.
I also commend the reasons the hon. member for Skeena presented, namely, that he wanted these papers to clear the names of certain persons. I would suggest humbly to the hon. member for Skeena that there is no agitation any longer. We have peace on the waterfront and Red McLaughlin, regardless of how Judge Norris castigated him, is at this very moment doing an adequate and satisfactory job, under the supervision of the trusteeship, as head of the S.I.U.
There is something more fundamental, and I think this really is what the motion is all about. I refer to the advisability of producing papers which are the property of the trustees. I think that as one of the better known lawyers of this country the hon. member for Bow River could have done a service to members such as myself and others if he had explained the rights of the trustees and how the very word "trust" or "trusteeship" is going to have any effect or validity in operation if we are going to destroy that trust which is implicit in the mandate of the trusteeship by taking confidential documents and correspondence between the Department of

Labour and the trustees in respect of the findings by the R.C.M.P. and their criticism of the S.I.U. and make them public periodically whenever anybody, well-intentioned or otherwise, asks for these documents. In that way the whole principle of the trusteeship would be destroyed.
The hon. member for Skeena did mention that it is not his normal practice to demand that the normal dealings of people, unions or business be made public for everybody to peruse, but he feels there are circumstances here which are more important involving the clearing of the names of certain individuals. I disagree with him. I think the whole question of the production of papers is a very contentious point under our parliamentary system. I have said this before. In this house we follow a pattern half way between the British and Swedish systems. I am sure most members are familiar with both systems. In Britain, as you know, the whole philosophy behind the production of papers is that everything is secret and only under exceptional circumstances are private papers or documents brought to public attention. The secrecy is so binding that not only does it apply to members of the House of Commons and members of the House of Lords but even to contractors who are doing jobs for the government in Great Britain. On the other hand, Sweden has a different philosophy and perhaps a more logical one in that everything is public with the exception of certain categories which are secret.
In Sweden they carry this to a logical conclusion, even to the extreme that in the cities of Sweden today, whether you are a newspaperman, a private citizen or a trade union man, you can go into large rooms in certain public buildings and demand or request, just like you do in a city library here, documents which under our system are considered secret. But even under this advanced method of dealing with documents and production of papers there are certain categories-four, if I recall accurately-which are considered to be secret and confidential and which cannot under normal circumstances be made public. The papers of the trusteeship fall into one of these categories. Therefore under the British system you would not get the papers and under the Swedish system, of which I approve because it spells out the conditions and categories in which papers are or are not available, papers such as the hon. member for Skeena has requested in good faith are not available.

As a matter of fact, in respect of the request by certain members of my own party I took the stand that certain documents should not be made public. I ruled against those hon. members, including I think one who will be speaking this evening. When it came to the specific papers which originated from the trustees I ruled, and I would rule again if I were in the same position, that you cannot have a trusteeship if you are going to take its papers and make them public. I am surprised that the hon. member for Bow River, who is a very experienced and senior member of the bar, should, of all speakers, not want to protect the rights of the trustees. I would think he would want to commend the fact that these papers are private.
The hon. member mentioned the fact that labour people are running around the country working for the New Democratic party. What about it? Labour in this country has the right to support whichever party it likes. Labour has as much right to support a political party as has big business to support the hon. member for Bow River. I see nothing wrong with that, nor do I see anything wrong with labour contributing to political parties just as big business contributes to the party of the hon. member for Bow River or any other party.
Since when has labour been denied the rights which other organizations have in this country? All of a sudden these contributions are bad because they came from one Hal Banks.

At this time that should be changed to the New York exchange. I continue:
-the management and control of Canada's foreign exchange and Canada's internal credit administration. As I see it, under this bill the private banks provide the capital for the day to day requirements of persons and industry in this country, usually on a reasonably short-term basis. That is the purpose of the bill, as I understand it. We all know that the banks do not lend the investors' money. It is very often said that they lend the money persons have deposited in the banks. We all know that they create capital by bookkeeping entries. That is recognized. Mr. Mackenzie King recognized that, as anyone can see who has read that speech in full, and others that he made.
We should combine these three pieces of banking legislation. As I see it, the Bank of Canada should provide the social capital required for all levels of government, based on our natural resources, our industrial equipment and on the capacity of the Canadian people to produce. That is the way credit is issued in the United States. It is issued on no other basis.
We cannot understand why we cannot use the Bank of Canada, as one segment of our banking system, to this effect. This social capital would provide the opportunity for the building of highways, hospitals, schools, parks and the carrying on of socialized industries and other services. That is the way this capital is raised at the present time, and I think it is most unfortunate-

It did seems to me that a good many of the quotations that he gave us related to the necessity for institutions that have since been established, such as the Bank of Canada, and that some of the fears that were expressed by those statesmen of long ago have been met by our modern financial machinery.
I do also want to thank the members of the house for their restraint, because one point most hon. members seemed to be agreed on was that it is highly desirable to approve this bill on second reading and to get it before the standing committee where testimony can be taken from bankers, from experts and from the public in general.
As might be expected, even in the brief speeches which have been made on second reading of this bill, there has been a good deal of repetition of what was said when the resolution was under discussion, but some new points were also made.
I would like to congratulate particularly the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) for his contribution. It is not often that members of this house are prepared to modify their views in the light of the discussion and in the light of their reflection upon the legislation as presented to the house. It was very gratifying to me as the minister sponsoring this bill to find the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands saying the following among other things: "There are compelling arguments for the removal of the 6 per cent limit, and again, "While, as I say, there are compelling reasons for its removal I have not found an economist who would dispute that statement".
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not say this in any way to gloat-not at all. I understand perfectly well that the hon. member was saying
[Mr. Herridge.I
a good deal more than that he agreed there were compelling arguments for removing the 6 per cent ceiling. I congratulate him because I think he has come to realize, as some of us who have been pondering this problem over some time, including the royal commissioners and other economists in this country, that whatever the 6 per cent ceiling on the bank interest rate did, it did not control the interest rates in this country. Therefore I felt that this was a most useful contribution to an understanding of the situation in which we now find ourselves.
The hon. member of course went on, as did some of his colleagues in the same party, to suggest that the Bank of Canada should be given power to regulate the rate of interest on loans and deposits. I do not agree with this suggestion but I can understand the reasons for it. I think it does mark an advance in the thinking of his party, that no longer are they concentrating on what I have always regarded as an obsolete and ineffective section of our present banking legislation, namely, the ceiling on bank interest rates.
I agree with several hon. members who have said that interest rates throughout the world are higher than is desirable. I said that in this house on September 8, and I said it in Washington. My views were echoed by almost every minister of finance in the civilized world. There has been undue reliance upon monetary policy, and I do hope that those who share my views and the views of other ministers of finance around the world will be equally prepared to support the kind of fiscal policies that are a better alternative.
I do not believe we can keep the rate of interest down by controls. It has been admitted in this house that to keep the rate of interest down by a 6 per cent ceiling on bank interest rates is not effective; neither do I think it would be effective to keep the general rate of interest down by law. What is important is to get a proper balance in the instruments for the stabilization of the economy, and I agree that too much reliance has been placed on monetary policy.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, there have been some criticisms that economic conditions have changed and that the time has come for our general approach to economic policy to be changed. The hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) today asked a question which he thought he might debate at ten o'clock tonight-I gather he is not going to do so. He did point to the fact that there had
October 6, 1966

Bank Act
been some decline in the index of industrial production in Canada in recent months. From that he drew the inference that there had been a general change in conditions and that we were now facing some sort of a down-turn in economic activity, and that therefore we should change our general monetary policy.
I would like to say a word or two about the present situation because there could be some misunderstanding if the impression created by the hon. member's remarks were to go unanswered. The decline in the industrial production index in July was accounted for by strikes in copper, nickel and iron ore operations. There were also strikes in other industries. All together 812,000 man hours were lost due to strikes in July, the equivalent of 0.65 per cent of estimated working time of the entire labour force. For manufacturing and mining, which are the two principal components of the industrial production index, the percentage of time lost due to strikes was higher. The decline in iron ore and non-ferrous metal mining amounted to 13 per cent. This alone was sufficient to reduce the total production index by one point. Manufacturing as a whole was steady in July, with non-durable goods production increasing by half a point and durable goods production being down by a half point. The decline in those last figures was associated with the earlier shut-down in the automobile industry for new model changes.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
The smaller rates of increase in total activity during the second quarter of 1966, which has also been remarked upon, were a natural consequence of the extraordinarily high rates achieved earlier in the year. The value of the gross national product increased by 4.4 per cent between the fourth quarter of 1965 and the first quarter of 1966. So that in the first quarter there was this extraordinary increase. This was far above any possible sustainable rate in the Canadian economy. In the first quarter the advance announcement of the Ontario sales tax increase caused some additional buying, and our exports to the United States in that quarter were very high, due to the very heavy demand at that particular time.
The adjustment from the extraordinary first quarter increase in the second quarter has been followed by a resumption of growth in many indicators in July and August. For example-and this is one of the most important of the economic indicators-there was a substantial increase in employment in August
and a decline in the unemployment rate. That cannot be associated in any way with a decline in economic activity. Automobile sales picked up strongly in July and August and total retail sales had recovered in June and July. Our exports continued to increase in July.
In general we are looking forward to a renewal of moderate increases in the gross national product in the third and fourth quarters of this year. With the economy fully employed it is difficult, indeed undesirable, to try to achieve the unsustainable rates of increase in the first quarter. Even, with the more moderate gains in economic activity compared with earlier in the year, pressure on prices and costs remains a serious problem and government policy is being followed to reduce the increases in prices that are troubling all of us.
I made these few remarks, Mr. Speaker, because they are relevant to some of the points made during the debate by speakers on various sides and because I did not want this particular question to go unanswered for more than a few hours.
The motion that was put and which was ruled out of order by you, Mr. Speaker, referred to the establishment of a new type of clearinghouse arrangement. I would draw attention to the comment that I made on July 5, 1966, when I was speaking on the resolution preceding this bill, when I said, as reported at page 7234 of Hansard:
The then minister-
I was referring to my predecessor.
-Indicated that the government intended to give further consideration to possible changes in the clearing system, including suggestions made by the royal commission, and would bring forward legislation on this general subject, which seems clearly to come within parliament's jurisdiction over banking. We still have this in mind for a future year.
I thought I should repeat these words, Mr. Speaker, in order to indicate that we are prepared to give consideration to one of the subjects raised by the motion that was ruled out of order.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when I introduced the proposed revision of the Bank Act I stated that one of the main objectives of the government was to improve the position of the small borrower. The government is convinced that an effective way to achieve this objective is to encourage and enforce competition, to implement a system where there are many competing sources of loan funds and many institutions freely competing for the custom of the consumer.

October 8, 1966
Bank Act
But the revision of the banking system and the introduction of more competition is not the only way the government intends to improve the position of the consumer who needs credit. Members will recall that on May 27 last I wrote to the provinces stating that I was prepared to convene a federal-provincial meeting on the subject of consumer credit and interest disclosure, which is so important to those Canadians who buy on instalment plan or who borrow from finance companies, banks or other sources. Since then officials of the Department of Finance have started to make preparations for such a conference and I hope to be able to announce to the house very shortly its agenda and date.
In the course of the discussions which we have had on this subject, it has occurred to me that there was an immediate opportunity for a breakthrough in one of the most important problems facing the consumers-that of the disclosure of the true and effective rate of interest. One of the basic aims of a consumer policy is to ensure that consumers have recourse to all the information necessary to make decisions that will be of greatest benefit to themselves and to the national economy.
Consumer groups and associations have urged for many years legislation requiring the cost of consumer credit of all kinds to be stated in terms of an effective annual or monthly rate of interest. Both the Nova Scotia and Ontario studies of consumer credit concluded that it was desirable and feasible for banks and other financial institutions to disclose the cost of borrowing both in dollar charges, as done at present, and also as an effective rate of interest. Nova Scotia, Ontario, Massachusetts and the United States federal government have all acted in this field in recent months.
I believe it to be of the highest importance that consumers buying on credit or borrowing for consumption have the fullest opportunity to know at what exact cost they are doing so.
I regard action on the disclosure of the effective cost of consumer credit extended by banks as a practical starting point for coordinated federal-provincial co-operation and development in this field. The banks are now the largest dispensers of consumer credit, and they can give us leadership in this field while we will be working on a more general approach at the federal-provincial conference.
In my recapitulation of the main proposals of the bank bill before you yesterday, I outlined the formula whereby the maximum rate of interest that banks may charge on 
loans in Canada would be made more flexible and eventually removed altogether. One of the technical effects of this amendment would be to remove any of the possible remaining problems of the banks in disclosing the cost of consumer credit transactions as an approximate effective percentage of the amount borrowed.
I think I might state at this time that among the amendments that the government will be putting before the house, which I mentioned at the conclusion of my first speech in the second reading debate, is an amendment, when this bill is in committee, which will require that a bank when making a consumer loan must state the effective rate of the combined cost of interest and service charges. In the committee there will be ample opportunity to consider the technical aspects of this proposal.
When this bill does receive second reading, Mr. Speaker, I would propose that it be referred to the standing committee on trade, finance and economic affairs.

speakeroldname: Hon. Maurice Sauve (Minisier of Forestry and Rural Development) moved

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-218, to provide assistance to livestock feeders in eastern Canada and British Columbia.
He said:

Mr. Speaker, it will be recalled that on June 30 the house passed the resolution without discussion and that first reading was given to the bill intituled: An act to provide assistance to livestock feeders in eastern Canada and British Columbia.
All parties had agreed that on second reading, all stages of the bill would be proceeded with.
That is why, today, my introductory remarks will be slightly longer than usual to fully inform members of this house of the aims of the bill and to give them other information on its contents.
The bill I am speaking on today is another landmark in the efforts undertaken by successive governments to allow the use of western feed grain, to improve its availability and to further stabilize its price in eastern Canada and British Columbia.
The bill providing assistance to livestock feeders calls for the establishment of a Canadian Livestock Feed Board which would ensure the availability of feed grain and adequate feed grain storage facilities in eastern Canada to meet the needs of livestock feeders, the reasonable stability of feed grain prices and a fair equalization of feed grain prices in eastern Canada and in British Columbia.
October 6, 1966
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)

A resolution containing a similar proposal had just been introduced by the former government under the initiative of Hon. Alvin Hamilton when the 1963 election was called.
Members of the house will recall that the standing committee on agriculture and colonization of the house which examined the feed grain pricing problem in 1964 recommended in its report on March 22, 1965 the creation of a feed grain agency. Since then, the implications of establishing this board and its relationship to other boards with responsibility in grain matters, have been assessed by the government. This evaluation led to the proposal you are being asked to consider this evening.

Freight assistance to feed grain and other grain products from the west to points of consumption in eastern Canada and in British Columbia was first started during the war, that is, in 1941.
That measure was passed because of the following situation: Breeders of eastern Canada and British Columbia maintained it was unfair that competing foreign breeders operating three or four miles away should obtain Canadian feed grain delivered in their countries at the same price or even at a lower price than that paid by Canadian breeders because of lower freight rates on grain exports. In addition, western grain markets were restricted due to the great risks endangering overseas shipments in wartime and because the allies required more concentrated foodstuffs.
The program served a double purpose: to expand the feed grain markets for the benefit of western grain producers and to enable farmers in eastern Canada and British Columbia to increase their cattle production.
Since the war, controls on wheat, oats and barley imports have deprived eastern cattle breeders of the opportunity to import grain at lower prices. Those factors, added to the concern of protecting investments made necessary by wartime needs, prompted government authorities to maintain this policy after the war. Since it also proved very profitable to western grain producers, it has been maintained and regularly extended through orders in council. The products eligible for assistance have changed little through the years, whereas the rates of freight assistance to
Canadian Livestock Feed Board various points have changed according to circumstances. The program required yearly appropriations ranging from $14.5 to $22 million.

In 1963 storage assistance was added to the program to encourage stocking of adequate supplies and as a means of moderating winter price movements. In the same year provisional pricing, formerly applied solely to wheat, was extended to oats and barley by the Canadian Wheat Board.
In 1964, in an effort to bring in truck competition and to allow for more effective bargaining on transportation rates on the part of local supplies, eastern Canada was divided into zones with a specific level of transportation aid applying to each zone. This part of the program has been particularly useful and has led to many and extensive rate readjustments.
Much concern is still expressed by feeders in eastern areas over fluctuations in feed prices. These result from a combination of factors including variations in supply and demand for western feed grains; changes in freight rates; shortage of winter storage space; paralysis of navigation in the winter; the holding supplies of certain pressure points in relatively few hands; price gyrations of other feed ingredients and to mounting retail mark-ups reflecting an increasing variety of services rendered at the retailing end of the feed business-credit, bagging, technical know-how, etc.

It is not easy to settle all those problems, since some of them overlap in the field of grain marketing. Up to now, the organization, purchase and distribution of grain stocks, as far as breeders are concerned, have been left entirely to trade.
The private sector has rendered many worthwhile services, but difficulties concerning stocks and prices have arisen and have been the subject of talks for some time.
In short, present programs concerning federal aid have not sufficiently dampened the unforeseeable and somewhat irregular movements of prices throughout the winter in eastern Canada as a result of the closing of the shipping season.
Eastern breeders have even asked the government to intervene to a greater extent in that field, in order to prevent unsteady prices, since otherwise feeding and production plans will be annihilated in a sector

October 6, 1966

Canadian Livestock Feed Board where the difference between costs and prices is almost always excessively reduced.
Cattle and fowl products represent three quarters of the financial income of eastern farms and 65 per cent of agricultural returns in British Columbia.
Agriculture which requires considerable manpower depends extensively on an ample supply of grass and fodder to which feed grain must be added. The vicinity of markets has also made the production of non-ruminant cattle profitable in surrounding areas of large consumption centres in eastern Canada, especially when considering that the areas adjoining Montreal and Toronto can very well lend themselves to an intensive grain production.
Cattle feeding represents an important current expense for farmers in eastern Canada and British Columbia. Outside the Prairies, a sum of $335 million is spent each year for the purchase of feed grain and seeds. The sale of feed grain in western Canada on those markets are just as important to the western farmer, since they represent about $110 million, of the farm income and contribute much toward the economic stability of the Canadian feed grain markets.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
The inability of provinces to meet their needs as far as grain is concerned varies from 70 to 80 per cent in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia to 17 to 20 per cent in Ontario and Prince Edward Island. Quebec meets about half its own needs, while British *Columbia is short by about a third. Livestock product markets are expanding rapidly. Consumers now tend to get away from starchy food and favour meat proteins. That is why a larger share of the consumer food budget is spent on livestock and poultry products.
By 1980, the estimated population in eastern Canada will likely need 140 per cent of the milk now produced in eastern Canada, 244 per cent of its poultry production, 180 per cent of its egg production, 218 per cent of its pork production and 440 per cent of its beef production.

How are these quickly evolving needs going to be met? If recent production trends can be of some guidance the situation for the last 14 years can be summarized as follows: From 1951 to 1964 the June 1 survey shows that the number of cattle, other than dairy cows and heifers, has increased by 120 per cent in
[Mr. Sauve.l
the prairie provinces, 80 per cent in Prince Edward Island, 58 per cent in Ontario and 22 per cent in Quebec, while remaining almost stationary in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
Over the same period there was a 29 per cent increase in the number of hogs. There was a slightly lower increase in the prairies, Quebec, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. Ontario's hog population does not show any definite trend, while New Brunswick's has dwindled by 37 per cent.
The total poultry population has increased tremendously in Nova Scotia and Quebec and, discounting shifts in types of poultry now kept, the other provinces are not showing any significant trend if we except Prince Edward Island which has witnessed a sizeable decrease of close to 60 per cent. The Quebec dairy herd is the only one holding the line, as the other provinces witness a continuous decline.
Should these trends continue in the near future, both east and west will be confronted by the additional food requirements I described a moment ago.

The increase in the number of livestock in each region will depend on such factors as the evolution of the market for grain and other products from the prairies, the evolution of meat markets in the United States, the extension of corn-growing land and the increase in the production of corn in the eastern and western part of the country, the improved conversion of livestock feed and the consumer demands with regard to freshness in the case of several agricultural products.
I introduce this bill today in this context and considering all these factors. The bill establishes a livestock feed board and an advisory committee. The board will act in the interest of livestock breeders and feeders in British Columbia and in the eastern part of the country by passing the necesary measures authorized by the law so as to ensure the availability of supplies and stockage at all times; it will also, as far as it is practical to do so, ensure a reasonable stability in prices and a fair equalization of freight charges.
In order to achieve these aims, the present aid policy concerning feed grain, and which extends to transportation and stocking, will become an integral part of the legislation. Even if the bill provides that the Canadian Livestock Feed Board shall deal with a considerable number of things, its first duty will
Oclober 6, 1966

Division BANK ACT
be to try to co-ordinate the various interests involved and, if necessary, to improve the means at its disposal. The aid provided for transportation may serve to encourage supply by water during the shipping season or by rail during the critical winter months. The board may negotiate the appropriation of adequate space in the elevators, as well as the establishment of lower rates of transport before rushing into large-scale marketing operations.
Should these means not succeed in achieving the objectives sought in this bill, the board may engage in purchasing, stocking, selling and other marketing operations. The use of such powers, should the need arise, shall be subject to an authorization by the governor in council, which would be valid for a definite time. There is a recommendation for the setting up, for the purposes of such marketing operations, of a $10 million automatically revolving fund. In case of need, when the fund is tied up in grain stocks, the governor in council may authorize the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) to make further advances.
The powers it is proposed to confer to the board do not extend to "prices ex warehouses, Fort William", but relate to marketing of feed grain from that stage of pricing to the eventual consumption of feed in eastern Canada and British Columbia.
This bill embodies a very necessary policy destined better to organize the transport of feed grain and ensure a more stable market for both grain products and livestock products. This is a necessity which we must face and we may rest assured that the government intends to pass other legislation or modify the present policy to meet the changing needs of grain producers and livestock breeders.
Those, Mr. Speaker, were the main points I wished to make on first reading of this bill. I shall make other comments later in answer to those which the hon. members will wish to make concerning this bill.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN STORAGE AND TRANSPORTATION COSTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now studying Bill C-218, an act to provide assistance to livestock feeders in eastern Canada and British Columbia. I listened carefully, although at times somewhat absent-mindedly, to the observations made by the minister of forestry (Mr. Sauve) when he introduced the bill. At the outset of the few remarks I wish to make this evening, I cannot help but remind the hon. minister that this measure is but the continuation of various legislative measures introduced by the Conservative government which preceded the present government.
In introducing this measure and giving the reasons for it, the present minister was in fact doing nothing else but addressing a word of reproach to his government. Indeed, he reminded us that a similar measure was on the agenda in 1963, that it had been proposed by the then minister of agriculture, the present member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton). We also know, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers have been expecting this bill for a long time.
It must also he recalled, Mr. Speaker, that at the time the hon. member for Qu'Appelle
(Mr. Speaker.)
October 6, 1966

(Mr. Hamilton) was minister of agriculture, he has travelled through the provinces, particularly Quebec and Ontario, to promote cattle raising. It is well known that in recent years, specially, there is a tendency in eastern Canada, as well as in other provinces, to use more beef. As a matter of fact, people who were using large quantities of pork regularly in the past have now changed their eating habits in favour of beef. There are a good many reasons for the increase of beef consumption in the feeding of humans and I certainly shall not labour over that part of the matter. But we must recognize the fact that beef consumption has greatly increased in recent years in Canada.
The event which will take place in Montreal during 1967 will also help to provide those of our farmers who are in the cattleraising business with a greatly enlarged market.
Even though, there may be cause for deploring the government's backwardness in adopting the necessary measures to encourage cattle raising in the eastern provinces, one must however rejoice in the fact that it has finally decided to tread the path which was cleared by the preceding government.
Mr. Speaker, one must not forget that the farmer's well-being in the east is in no way an obstacle to the well-being of the farmer out west and conversely, it is also true that the western farmers are not at a disadvantage when their brothers in the east prosper.
It is a well-known fact that farmers, because of the constantly increasing cost of living, find it very hard to meet their obligations. The government should therefore take every opportunity to help this sector of our country's economy.
Anybody who has followed a little closely the change in the farmer's attitude knows for a fact that the latter has finally decided to take a more personal interest in the management of his own business. He has now taken cognizance of his own general responsibilities and has decided to participate more actively in the marketing of his products and in the things which affect his income and his welfare. That is why farmers, whenever they get together at conventions, consider more closely than they used to bills introduced here. And when the minister announced some time ago the abolition of free winter storage of feed grain in reserved space in eastern elevators, there was a general outcry against his decisions and farmers protested most energetically.
Canadian Livestock Feed Board
Mr. Speaker, it would not be logical for the minister to introduce, on the one hand, a measure intended to encourage the breeding of beef-type cattle if, on the other hand, he moved other legislation to deprive breeders of the grain they need to feed such cattle in winter. I know the minister received, like so many members of the house, a telegram of protest from the Quebec millers, supported by the Catholic Farmers Union.
I am sorry I do not have with me a copy of the telegram. But I can surely give the minister the copy I was sent when I have time to go to my office.
Mr. Speaker, the arrangements made by the minister also amazed me-you may feel that I am out of order here-but as feed grains are concerned the matter was studied specifically at the special meeting held in Drummondville, it seems to me the minister could have extended invitations not only to the members of the cabinet but to the other representatives of the area who are bent also on seeing an objective study made of livestock raising.
He attempted systematically to keep the members of the opposition out; maybe it is fair play as far as he is concerned, but I think that he has therefore done a disservice to the cattle breeders of my riding and the surrounding counties.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, there are still many points that we would like to clarify in this measure; it is not necessary to state all the objections, to undertake a detailed study at this stage of discussion, because we will certainly have the opportunity to look at it more closely. Then we shall make the necessary comments, and also offer suggestions because if we study the past achievements of the Conservative party especially in that field, we feel that we can justly claim a certain knowledge in this matter and I do think that the members of the opposition will offer to the minister suggestions which will certainly help him to carry out a policy which was initiated under his predecessor.
I know that the minister of forestry who is responsible for the administration of this legislation is broad-minded, that he wants to improve the well-being of the farmers and that, for that reason, it will be impossible for him logically to ignore the suggestions which will come from this side of the house.
October 6, 1966

Canadian Livestock Feed Board
Until we have the opportunity to say more about it, I wish the minister well in the discharge of his duties.

speechtext:
I rise to express briefly the support of this party of the principles and purposes of the measure before us.
I listened to the minister's remarks with interest, and having read the bill through carefully I think it is fair to say that at heart the minister is somewhat of a socialist. This measure reminds me of the early efforts of some of the agriculture organizations in the interior of British Columbia to get the government to take action along these lines, to equalize the cost of grain required for livestock and poultry production. There was an effort in the Fraser Valley toward this end and it is safe to say that the agriculture organizations of British Columbia were in the van of the movement to get some measure of financial assistance from the federal government toward the cost of grain transportation. At that time the question of storage was not mentioned.
I have attended many meetings at which this subject has been discussed. In the district I have the honour to represent we are severely affected by the high price of grain in the circumstances in which livestock and poultry are produced. I know that when this measure was first proposed some people suggested that we were advocating socialism. It was considered then an advanced form of legislation. Regardless of that, we are very glad to see it passed because this legislation will do something to bring a measure of equality to production costs as between various agricultural producers from one end of Canada to the other.
I presume it is correct to say that this is in the nature of experimental legislation, and that experience will provide an opportunity for improvements to be made. In this connection I am glad to see that it will be the duty of the board which is to be established to make a continuing study of feed grain requirements in eastern Canada and British Columbia, of the availability of feed grain and of the requirements for additional feed grain storage facilities in those areas. I am always anxious that legislation of this type should be followed up and that reports should be made to the minister and to the House.

I am glad to see it will be the duty of the board to make recommendations to the minister with respect to requirements for additional feed grain storage facilities in eastern. Canada; also, that generally it will be the duty of the board to advise the government on all matters pertaining to the stabilization and fair equalization of feed grain prices to livestock feeders. It is also good to note that the board will be required, to the greatest possible extent consistent with its objects, to consult and co-operate with all departments, branches or other agencies of the government of Canada or of any province having duties related to, or having aims or objects related to, those of the board.
It is my belief that if this legislation is to work satisfactorily there must be co-operation with the provincial departments concerned, with the farmers organizations and with all those who are directly affected. This is why the last provision to which I referred is particularly welcome.
I notice, too, that the governor in council may from time to time empower the board to make inquiries and investigations in respect of-
- (a) transportation, storage or handling of feed grain in eastern Canada and British Columbia.
(b)	supplies and prices of feed grain in such areas, and
(c)	payments related to the cost of feed grain storage or transportation made under this act.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I mention this particularly because I think it is essential in this type of legislation to have a follow-up and a continuing investigation of its effect on the farmers concerned, of its effect on the economy generally, the surrounding economy, and naturally of its cost to the government of Canada, and so on. I do not think there is any necessity for me to speak at length except to say I am confident that the agricultural producers who will be affected by this legislation will welcome it and do their best to co-operate with the government and all other agencies in making it a success.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with some anxiety mixed with pleasure that we listened to the minister's statement when he introduced Bill No. C-218. It had been eagerly awaited in this house for several years and a great deal has already been said on this matter.

October 6, 1966	COMMONS
After the board is established by this house, and everything will have been said, at least in principle, in this connection, the task of the minister responsible for it will not necessarily be completed. On the contrary, it will then be his duty to see that the bill is implemented most efficiently. Even though the bill contains some regulations, things are often different in theory from what they are in practice.
And I think that due to past experience, the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development, the sponsor of this bill, is well-informed and satisfactorily advised in that field. However, I take the liberty of drawing his attention to a few points which could perhaps serve him as guide lines, not for all practical purposes but in general, if you prefer, to some objections which could be raised on this side of the house and which he could take in consideration and study thoroughly, namely if it would not be a fair and profitable solution for the government as well as for the board and the farmers involved.
Mr. Speaker, there are clauses in that bill which are worthwhile, but there are others which make me feel uneasy. It is perhaps because I have not had time to study the bill as thoroughly as I would have liked to. Evidently, I will have an opportunity to do so during consideration in committee.
Nevertheless, I wish to draw the attention of the minister to certain provisions for obtaining such feed grain as far as eastern Canada and British Columbia are concerned.
I see that by this bill, the minister tries as much as possible to cut prices, that is to make feed grain available at a reasonable price to our farmers of eastern Canada, and heaven knows that they need it. However, an attempt must be made to find out how this result can best be attained.
I already mentioned some time ago in this house the mechanism which now prevails. I believe I asked the minister to keep an eye open to prevent unscrupulous individuals from using an agency responsible to the government. Unscrupulous persons used in the past certain devious means, which were not very orthodox, as it were, or means not altogether in keeping with Christian principles, to take advantage of this scheme to the detriment of western and eastern farmers. At a certain time, producers of western Canada were reported as saying: We do not get enough for our grain because eastern farmers and stock breeders do not want to pay.
DEBATES	8427
Canadian Livestock Feed Board And eastern farmers and stock breeders were saying: We cannot get feed grain at a reasonable price because western producers make a prohibitive profit.
In the end, who is right? Is it because one does not have the means to pay enough or because the other asks too much? And that is the problem which will always occur. Now it is the object of that agency to have enough feed grain at home to meet the needs first and then to have them at a reasonable price. Therefore, I am interested in finding out from the minister what means, will be used to distribute this grain once it reaches eastern Canada?
Of course, the livestock feed board will have its say. But it does not mean, for instance, that it will be the one responsible for carrying grain from the lakehead to eastern Canada elevators. There is somebody else who will have a finger in the pie, who will mess about in it. Now, I want to know who will mess about in there, who will fiddle about with it. Unless action is taken now, it will be found that the same situation will repeat itself, as was the case with western Canada in 1936, and which brought about the establishment of the present Canadian Wheat Board, which at least set out standards and which guaranteed an income to western farmers and producers.
On the other hand, it does not mean that speculators have been eliminated. Granted, producers were guaranteed a cost price, but what about speculators?
Have they been removed? Have we passed a law with enough teeth in it to protect western producers against being exploited by such people? And now this is what I would like to know. I am not sure whether the Canadian Wheat Board has managed to quench this speculation which was detrimental to western farmers. It has been contained at the head of the Great Lakes, but not removed entirely; on the other hand, the Board took control of production over there, exactly as the feed grain board can take control over here as far as purchases and distribution of feed grain to eastern feeders are concerned. But if speculation is not checked, the situation will go from bad to worse because there will be a go-between which will become a white elephant and which will cost the Canadian taxpayer a lot of money and the problem will not have been solved. If the price of grain increase or remain the same, there is no need in that case, to set up
3428	COMMONS
Canadian Livestock Feed Board a board to do what we are doing now. But I think that the minister is wise enough to keep a close watch on the openings through which speculators might sneak in. At least I hope so, because if we do not take steps to prevent as much as possible the payment of a commission here and a commission there through lack of organization in the distribution of such feed grain, we might as well not have any at all. And I think that the minister will keep an eye for such loopholes.
Should I notice at any time that there is a leak somewhere, it would be my duty to warn the minister. The same goes for all those here in the house. On the other hand, it is the minister's duty to take all the necessary precautions to avoid leaks. And here I think of some wholesalers, if you wish not only brokers because there are others who are not members of the exchange. As a matter of fact, I did not quite like the solution applied by the Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. Speaker, and if ever I am told that the Canadian Wheat Board will be linked to that body called the livestock feed board for eastern Canada, I will have some things to say about that. For instance I can say that the Canadian Wheat Board guarantees and negotiates prices very well but it does not necessarily see to the delivery. It is still asking the advice of some brokers it has kept away since 1936 from the purchasing field in western Canada. And that is what is called the grain exchange. It probably has its uses for speculations on the world market and all that, but I am against its speculating at the expense of Canadians in the central provinces.
Moreover, the Canadian Wheat Board has to turn to the members of the grain exchange to inquire about futures prices, that is, as anyone who is a wheat or feed grower in western Canada knows, the price quoted in the spring for such and such feed grain to be delivered in the fall in order to make an immediate sale. Grain is sold at a fixed price or a pre-fixed price if you wish. On the other hand, who is asked to set up that price? The brokers. And who buys in the fall, quite often the brokers.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
They are not fools, Mr. Speaker, they are speculators. And if they intend to make a penny, a dollar on that, they will see to it that they make it. They just have to say: oats will sell for 67 cents this fall; on the other hand, one finds out that it sold through them for 75 cents afterwards. Therefore who

DEBATES	October 6, 1966
lost on that? Of course, there is always the question of rebate on sales paid immediately or in the fall then. But the future price is fixed. The price is set, the feed is sold at that price, which is then reduced at the expense of the western or eastern farmer. But the broker does not sell it at this price and he is the one who determines whether the harvest is to be good or bad and in a sense informs the Canadian Wheat Board. This does not mean that the wheat board does not work well but it could perhaps extend its scope a little further to give western producers a larger income. The feed grain board which will be established in my region could perhaps buy directly from the farmer without going through some broker or speculator. Of course, there would be a conflict of interest. We would have two commissions under the jurisdiction of the same government. It would have been better perhaps to have put this under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments, because negotiations, what is called "bargaining value", are involved. On the other hand, it is incumbent on the minister to find means to provide such feed grain at the lowest possible price or cheaper for the benefit of the livestock feeders in eastern Canada. And if such aim were not achieved, the board could not justify its existence. Unless we see to it that the goal be reached, we have lost our time in this house, the taxpayer's money has been dilapidated and we have fallen short of the expectations of eastern Canada livestock feeders.
I think we might have to sing the same song in eastern Canada and in western Canada; to put our backs into it once and for all; to indicate exactly the price that the farmers or the producers in western Canada obtain for their wheat, or get for their feed grain, or earn for the grain sold on the home market, in order that the eastern Canada farmer may know exactly how much the other farmer has received at the opposite end of the country.
Mr. Speaker, in this case, we find a differential of $2, $3, $4, and even $5 per hundredweight. You might find this amazing. Wait a moment, and you will hear things even more amazing. Let us consider the case of the western Canada producer who ships to Fort William, in what we call carloads, grain that bears dockage on arrival at Fort William. They remove what is commonly called wild oats, the straw, the chaff, whatever residues
October 6, 1966
there might be. They simply do not look for grain but for anything that might be found besides grain.
The dockage may vary between J, 2, 3 or 5 per cent. All this is removed and not paid for. This is called "dockage".
On the other hand, the farmer is not paid for that; yet he is asked to pay transportation charges on it from the elevators out west to the lakehead or Fort Churchill. He is not paid for it when it is taken away, but elsewhere, mills pay $2.35 and $2.70 per hundredweight for it.
Wild oats, chaff, straw and hulls come first, that is, what farmers are not paid for; yet, it is good enough for feed? That explains, up to a point, why feed is so expensive. Stock breeders in eastern Canada surely cannot feed their pigs, sheep, cattle, horses and milking cows with chaff and other fodder without food value; consequently, all kinds of ingredients are added to their feed. Each time ingredients are added, the price goes up; prohibitive prices are charged and feed ends up by costing how much? $4.50! But that type of feed is not very good, that is not the one which gets the best publicity either. Publicity is for the $5, $5.50 and $6 bags. Finally, why is it sold at $6 per hundredweight when the farmer out West did not believe it was any good, and did not get much for it? It was classed as "dockage" at the head of the great lakes.
Mr. Speaker, I would like the hon. minister to watch these grain transport operations and transactions. Let us first begin by putting into the feed which is sold in eastern Canada, ingredients which will provide our stock with the necessary vitamins.
They will perhaps have to put less of other things into it in order to obtain a reasonable price to sell our feed to our farmers, to enable our livestock breeder to buy that feed at reasonable prices.
He will have a field of about 70, 80 or 100 acres, he will harvest it, leaving 30 acres to be sold, for this deprives him of the wheat market. What is he going to do with it? It sells for 56 cents, 60 cents, 70 cents, 75 cents a bushel, not a hundredweight but a bushel. You are going to get oats weighing how much? Maybe 52, 53, 54, 55 pounds a bushel. This is not oats that was nipped by frost, not oats to feed poultry that I am referring to, but registered seed oats; and western farmers and members in this house are well aware of that.
Canadian Livestock Feed Board
How is it that oats of that kind is very often being brought to our area-that is not what is being sold to them as seed oats-at $5, $6 or $7 a hundredweight.
How come? Did the western farmer or producer not pay the freight from Fort William out of the 70 cents or 75 cents he gets a bushel? Is freight that expensive from Fort William to the province of Quebec? Does it really cost that much to supply oats or grain at a reasonable price to eastern farmers? Perhaps, along the way, unscrupulous people take advantage of the situation to make a few dollars. I am therefore asking the minister to see to it that such intervention is stopped, as well as anything which would permit those people to further speculate under the cover of any federal or provincial board; in short, let us put teeth in the law which will break them once and for all.
The western farmer or producer must be treated fairly, but the eastern breeder must also receive fair treatment; one must pay exactly what he ought, the market value, and the other must receive exactly what he should for his grain on the Canadian market. Let us not be so concerned with the establishment of external markets; let us begin by satisfying our domestic market, then we will sell outside. We now have some good domestic contracts; we sell right and left, and this is excellent. By their bountiful harvest this year, the western producers have proved they can produce. Western Canada this year had what may be called its record harvest.
They have proved they can produce, and now it is up to us to prove that we can, and soon, market their production, to the advantage of the eastern producer as well as that of the world at large, where exports are concerned. But this can be achieved only when we have legislation to block, once and for all, any attempt or possibility of speculation, on foreign as well as domestic markets, and to guarantee fairness or a fair price to the producers and buyers of these grains. That is why we will tackle the problem again and study each and every item of the bill when it comes before the committee.
In the meantime, we shall study it, and if need be, suggest what amendments should be made.
