Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Sauve), who

Canadian Livestock Feed Board will be responsible for administering the provisions of Bill No. C-218, is well aware that what is being done by the provisions now before us is more important than the powers and responsibilities granted to the agency to be set up.
I rise tonight, not to advance categorical or unequivocal opposition to the establishment of this agency, but simply to caution the minister to make sure that in the application of the powers granted to the agency we do not create an unnatural imbalance of opportunities in various regions of Canada. This could be possible-and I talk not only about the imbalance in respect of livestock feeding but also in respect of grain producing. I am not the only one who has that opinion. Earlier this year discussions were held in Winnipeg regarding what was referred to as the feed grain dilemma. Some of the excerpts I wish to read are taken from speeches delivered to the Seventh National Farm and Business Forum.
During the course of meetings of a committee which studied this whole matter I was instrumental in moving a motion to the effect that a study should be made of prices being paid by livestock producers in eastern Canada and British Columbia. I have a great deal of sympathy for the problems that these people face toward the end of their feeding season, notably in February and March. Something in addition to what is being done should be done by the federal government to protect the stability of the feed prices these feeders must pay, not only at the end of the season but right from the beginning. In this way they could be sure when they undertake to feed cattle in October or November they would be able to purchase feed and grain to the end of the feeding season without being held up, or in some way suffer losses because of exorbitant prices.
We have heard some pretty convincing evidence which indicates that as soon as the seaway is closed the price of western grain in eastern Canada is increased by almost exactly the increase in transportation costs, in spite of the fact that this grain has been transported to eastern Canada by the cheapest possible means and stored.
Let me get back to this matter referred to as the feed grain dilemma. I want to quote from a speech made by Mr. Bert Hargrave, who is a leading agriculturist in Alberta and has been associated with many farm and

October 6, 1966
ranching organizations there. In his concluding remarks he said that-
-Canadians would soon have to forget their political differences and to realize that beef would have to be produced and finished in the most economic and efficient location. Artificial barriers or stimulants would eventually only upset other aspects of agriculture at increased public expense.
I suggest this is a valid point of view although it does perhaps place more emphasis on the interests of one region in Canada as against another. It must be remembered that Mr, Hargrave has represented beef producers in southern Alberta for some time.
I was rather surprised by this statement which appears in a speech delivered by Dr. Cecil B. Haver of the department of agricultural economics, Macdonald College, Ste. Anne de Bellevue, Quebec. In summing up he said:
The benefits of the feed freight program in the east . . . have largely gone to the big feeders and the big commercial users.
I am not surprised that he takes this attitude, but I suggest we must keep in mind, when setting up national policies involving the expenditure of money from the national treasury, the kind and size of farm we wish to help. If we find that our assistance is being provided to big feeders and commercial users we are perhaps misallocating public funds because we are using subsidies to produce beef, pork, or what have you, in regions where it is uneconomic to do so.
For those in this house who are not familiar with this feed freight policy perhaps it would be of benefit to draw their attention to the number of cattle fed in Ontario and in Quebec which are imported from western Canada. These live animals are freighted in. Then if you ship the grain from western Canada down here, where the feeding ratio of pounds of grain is away above that of the number of pounds of beef, in order to fatten the cattle, it is far less economical than feeding the grain to the animal in an area where both are produced and the carcasses are later shipped here in the form of meat. We have to take these things into consideration.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Dr. J. C. Gilson, head of the Department of Agricultural Economics, University of Manitoba, had this to say. This is not an exact quote, but it is very nearly what he said:
It was necessary to ask, bad the policy, in fact contributed to the development of the livestock industry in eastern Canada? What justification was

October 6, 1966	COMMONS
there for a national agricultural policy which helped one group of livestock producers at the expense of another? Were there not more direct and more effective means of dealing with the development of the livestock industry in eastern Canada?
I suggest that this is true so far as the national policy is concerned in that assistance to this group of feeders in eastern Canada has more or less been confined to freight assistance plus some storage. Perhaps the setting up of an agency that will have control throughout the whole feeding season, and also control of the price all through the feeding season, is another matter to which Dr. Gilson was referring. I am happy to say that this is a very important part of the bill before us.
However, in addition to the feed grain dilemma we must give consideration to the situation of the feed grain producers in Ontario and Quebec, because to the extent that additional subsidies are paid on western grain being brought in to this part of the country, their price is depressed. At least the demand for their product is lessened in these areas. I should like to read another quotation from this conference. For example, the following is given as Dr. Gilson's opinion:
He was almost tempted to conclude, that all the feed freight assistance policy had accomplished for the livestock industry in eastern Canada during the past 20 years had been to provide an incentive for a reduction in the quantity of locally grown grains.
That is a pretty severe conclusion, but I have to agree that there is some validity in it, because since freight assistance on feed grain was instituted, I believe in 1944 or somewhere around that time, there has been a marked decline in the volume of feed grains produced in eastern Canada, particularly in eastern Ontario and Quebec. Therefore we have to take this question into consideration.
I am sure there are a large number of farmers in Ontario and Quebec who depend for their livelihood on the price of the feed grains that they produce. As far as I am concerned, these people are just as important as those who depend upon the production of beef, pork or broilers in the poultry industry.
I am not going into a great deal of detail as to the provisions of this bill, because as I said at the outset-and I am sure the minister would agree-what is important is not so much what is in the bill but how its provisions are applied. I would give a word of caution in this respect. When a vehicle such as this is set up whereby government subsidies are advanced from time to time, and 23033-533
DEBATES	8431
Canadian Livestock Feed Board even increased from time to time to the advantage of one group, it may on occasion be tempting to allow these subsidies for one reason or another. Therefore when the minister administers the operation of this feed grain agency I think he will have to bear in mind constantly the impact on the whole country of any temporary change. He will not only have to bear in mind the impact on the whole country but on the farmers in the eastern region who may have a difference of interest, in that some would be more interested in a high price for feed grain and some would be more interested in a low price.
It may be tempting to solve local or temporary problems in this way because of pressure applied by a particular group. It may be tempting to increase subsidies for this reason, but I would hope caution would be used in this respect.
There is one other point of which I think the minister is probably aware, but I should like to draw it to his attention because I think it is important. I refer to the position of the feed grain producer in western Canada. I believe it is fair to say that if there had never been any feed grain freight assistance policy a large number of feed grains now being shipped from western to eastern Canada would never have started coming here, because there are large quantities of corn and other grains available in the United States that are closer to eastern Canada. In spite of the small duty, the competition from these grains in relation to grains from western Canada would have worked against the shipment of feed grains from western Canada to this part of the country. But we also have what at the present time seems to be a chronic problem, namely that of our international balance of payments. Our whole economy benefits and our problem in respect of international balance of payments is alleviated with every dollar's worth of goods, be it feed grain or anything else, that is produced and used in Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say to the minister that there are many, many contrary interests involved in what is contemplated in this feed grain agency. I hope that when the agency begins operations the minister will keep in mind the whole of Canada, rather than attempting to use the agency to satisfy some temporary local problem that may be raised.
Perhaps it would be more appropriate to discuss some of the powers of the board at another time, but I am concerned about one or two of the powers that will be granted to
October 6, 1968

Canadian Livestock Feed Board this agency. For example, on page 3 of the bill, clause 6 (c) says that the board may, in furtherance of its objects, allocate space reserved for its use in any storage facility among persons requiring feed grain storage facilities in eastern Canada. My understanding at the moment is that all the terminal elevators along the St. Lawrence river, in so far as priorities and allocations for specific purposes are concerned, are now in the hands of the Board of Grain Commissioners. It seems to me that the authority given to this feed grain agency to allocate or reserve space will have to be applied in such a way that it does not conflict with the powers now in the hands of the Board of Grain Commissioners. It seems to me, also, that one will have to be very careful about balancing these priorities. The word "balancing" always enters into these discussions, because I think eastern feeders have as much right to some of the storage facilities as the western farmers have to a large part of the storage for overseas shipments of wheat during the winter months.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
And so it seems to me that perhaps one of the best ways of resolving this problem is to give some kind of joint power, or at least require that some negotiations take place between these two agencies so that they can take into account the interest of both the groups concerned. As is provided later on in clause 6, I think it is useful for this board to conduct a continuing study of prices, feed grain consumption and handling and shipping facilities, because one of the difficulties has been in getting accurate information on how much grain is in store at the end of the season, how much should have been put in store and what was the price, taking into account all the factors contributing to that price, and then to see what happens to that price later on during the feeding season. There has been contradictory evidence, but if we had an agency set up to conduct a continuing study and to assemble all the facts and figures, it would certainly be useful.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, my main purpose is to caution the minister and the administration because I regard this bill as a means of providing a useful agency which will render a service to Canada and to many Canadians. On the other hand if the minister, the agency or the government should yield to some of the temptations held out to them from a certain group it could turn out to be one of the most discriminatory and harmful


agencies that has ever been set up by this parliament. I rely on the minister to use sound judgment in the application of the powers that are involved in this bill.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE IN STORAGE AND TRANSPORTATION COSTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like most other hon. members who have spoken during the debate on Bill C-218 so far this evening, I should like to commend the minister on the introduction of this legislation. As the minister is undoubtedly aware, there are certainly mixed feelings in western Canada about the efficacy or desirability of bringing in this particular legislation. I myself, as a representative of a western agricultural constituency, have mixed feelings, but my reservations with respect to this legislation are not of sufficient degree to warrant my voting against it.
I certainly intend to support the establishment of a feed purchasing agency, my major reason being that the farmers of eastern Canada and British Columbia certainly deserve this kind of support from the government. After all it has how been several decades since the producers of western Canada have had the advantage of having their grain products handled by a crown grain handling agency, the action stipulated in this measure would seem merely to be a just action on the part of the government at this time. If one region of the country is to be given the advantages of a certain action by the government, such as the establishment by the crown of a grain handling agency, then other regions of the country should be entitled to the same kind of consideration and treatment if the economics warrant it.
To the best of my knowledge there have been conflicting opinions coming from a number of professional economists, some saying that there was scant justification for this kind of assistance and others quite firm in the opinion that there was an economic basis for it. The pattern seemed to me to be dependant upon what part of the country the particular economist came from. Certain agricultural organization spokesmen from western Canada, and one or two prairie ministers of agriculture, have expressed fairly strong opposition to this proposed legislation. Then again, there have been some-notably one Alfred Gleave, former president of the National Farmers Union-who, on several occasions over the past year has come out in support of the concept of a crown feed purchasing agency and also for the continuation of feed grain freight assistance.
October 6, 1966
Mr. Speaker, I realize it is very close to ten o'clock, but rather than call it ten o'clock and hold my remarks over until the next day, I would like to try to conclude in the next 60 seconds or so by simply saying to the minister that if there is opposition to this legislation, from certain quarters, there is at the same time a genuine need for the legislation in eastern Canada and in British Columbia. There is also support for it in western Canada, in the prairies, on the basis that what is being provided here is simply an extension of the benefits which have been extended to western producers over the course of many years.
Of course, I could ask a very valid question: Why is it that eastern purchasers of feed grain have not deemed it worth while to attempt to establish co-operative agencies for the purchasing of feed grains? After all, in western Canada several decades ago it was deemed advisable and necessary to do just that, to establish co-operative agencies for the handling of grain, and it has proved to be of great and immediate tangible value to the farmers. It seems to me that in like manner this would have been the case with respect to the purchase of grain in eastern Canada. However, it may well be that the logistics of organizing this kind of co-operative agency is simply beyond the scope and capacity of the co-operative groups existing in eastern Canada at this time.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I heartily concur in and am in complete accord with what was already said by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), namely that it is not so much the legislation as the way in which the statute and regulations under it are applied that is important. This will determine whether or not the producers, and in particular the smaller farmers of eastern Canada, will get any real benefits or advantages from this policy or this legislation. We, the producers of western Canada will certainly be looking very closely at this agency and at how it works out in the course of the next year or two. If it comes to light that the ones who are really benefiting from the legislation are the virtually integrated livestock producers of the east, or that it is the distributors and speculators in feed that are benefiting to a larger degree, then of course this legislation will be deemed a failure. Therefore of course much remains to be seen. In the meantime our support is extended for BiU C-218.

HISTORIC SITES-QUEBEC-DEMOLITION OF HOME OF SIR ALEXANDER GALT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks to make concerning the question I put yesterday to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing). Could the minister tell us why he ordered the demolition of Sir Alexander Galt's house in Sherbrooke, without giving notice to the Eastern Township Historical Society, and whether he intends to honour the memory of this Father of Confederation by restoring the remaining outbuildings?
Several months ago, the minister responsible for the national historic sites division agreed with the Quebec government, in the framework of centennial celebrations, to honour the memory of Sir Alexander Galt by restoring his old house which still stood in Sherbrooke until recently.
I leave it to the minister to indicate why he has ordered the demolition of that house. What I blame him or his officials for, is having ordered the demolition without having previously given notice to the Eastern Township Historical Society and the federal member for Sherbrooke who are greatly interested in the carrying out of the project.
I hope the minister will nevertheless authorize

The project must be carried into effect, from both the historical and the confederative point of view, and I wish to draw the attention of the house to the great disenchantment of millions of Canadians, and particularly to that of the English speaking minority in Quebec, in the eastern townships and in Sherbrooke.

subtopic: HISTORIC SITES-QUEBEC-DEMOLITION OF HOME OF SIR ALEXANDER GALT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Sherbrooke for having raised this matter. I also want to assure him that I have received a considerable number of questions, and indeed complaints, from a variety of sources, including the hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Asselin) who has brought this situation to my attention a number of times during the past week.
I regret the occurrence very much indeed because apparently, as a result of the attempt to move this building, we have destroyed a house of one of the fathers of confederation, what was unquestionably an historic building of very great significance in the country.
I should like to tell the hon. gentleman what has gone on. This proposal goes back to 1962 when there was a private request for preservation of Galt House. My board-that is, the Historic Sites and Monuments Board -at that time approved the plan and said it was worth while saving, but no one came forward to participate.
In August, 1963, we again concurred, but asked that the matter of Galt House be kept over until we had had a look at the homes of as many of the fathers of confederation as we could possibly find in the various provinces, because there had been a suggestion that they should be preserved.

DEBATES	October 6, 1966
On February 4, 1965, we had a telephone call from the Dominican Sisters, whose property it was, telling us that they were going to move the house or demolish it in any case because they were expanding their own property and wondered whether we were interested. At the same time we had correspondence from the Eastern Townships Historical Society, who appealed to the Quebec government at that time that the Quebec Commission for Historical Sites be asked to participate. They wrote a letter to Hon. Carrier Fortin on July 24 and received a letter from him saying that they would participate.
On December 10, 1965, the president of the Eastern Townships Historical Society, Mr. Bachand, wrote to the department setting out their efforts to save the house. On March 3, 1966, Hon. Carrier Fortin expressed the first indication that the provincial government was willing to enter into an agreement with the federal government to assume 50 per cent of the restoration cost. This was confirmed by him in a letter on April 5, 1966.
On April 27 the department wrote to Hon. Carrier Fortin pointing out that if the province would not participate to the extent of maintenance, we could not carry the building ourselves. We therefore requested that the city of Sherbrooke participate. Sherbrooke became involved on July 29 and agreed to assume part of the cost, if we removed the building.
Later on, at about the end of July, we were informed by the Dominican Sisters of the fact that on August 8 they intended to begin demolishing the building. Thereafter we made a very great effort-a hurried effort-to put in a contractor. We got a report which said that the old house could be moved. It is a brick dwelling sitting on 50 per cent bedrock. We were told it could be moved, and we proceeded to move it. We did not get very far.
This house has heard the story of the doctor and the operation. Here, neither the operation nor the consequences of it were successful. I think we have learned that it is probably impossible to move a brick house off that type of foundation when the mortar is 100 years old. The building collapsed. We were confronted with the possibility of losing the house, and naturally, an attempt was made to move it. We attempted to move it, and the attempt failed.

SHIPPING-BALA, ONTARIO-OBSTRUCTION OF NAVIGATION BY BRIDGE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
This afternoon I asked a question concerning wharf access. It is an urgent matter and involves an important principle.
Briefly stated, authority has been granted for the Canadian National to instal a fixed bridge in substitution for a swing bridge over Jeannette's Narrows on Lake Muskoka, which will close off all but small boat navigation to the wharf at the town of Bala, which is a town deriving most of its income from tourist traffic and the boat trade.
Moreover, a Privy Council order No. 1907 of 1965, and a Board of Transport Commissioner's order No. 121124 of June 17, 1966, were made without public or private notice to those affected.
Finally, the Canadian National serlt in a crew to convert the bridge, while efforts were being made to delay the conversion.
For 75 years excursion boats have carried passengers on the Muskoka lakes. The town of Bala was a regular calling place. There was, and still is, a large wharf at Bala, and within the past several years it has been rebuilt. The approaches have been improved and extensive funds have been spent.
The excursion boat traffic went into decline, and about eight years ago Bala was discontinued as a port of call. The navigation company closed down. Where the mistake was made, I believe, was that after this wharf had been disused for some time it was assumed that it would never be used again for its previous purpose. It has now come about that use is requested of the wharf. Last year, Muskoka Excursions Limited put a large new excursion ship, the Miss Muskoka, on the lake. This year a second ship the Lady Muskoka was added to the fleet. Excursion ships and excursion boats have now resumed plying the lakes. The town of Bala, and the ship owners have arranged to have the ships call at Bala wharf.
On July 20 of this year the town of Bala applied to the Canadian National for permission to open the swing bridge. It was then that the existence of the orders I have referred to became known.
I have raised this question because the government has acquiesced in what is being done under a privy council order. In closing this means of navigation permanently, there is no alternate way for boats to come in to the Bala wharf.

If this had not been a government department the transaction would have been illegal under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. However, the government has the authority to make such an order, and it did so. My complaint is that the application was not founded on a proper basis and that an opportunity was not given to those interested to be heard and to explain what might happen in the future. I am asking the government now what means of access they intend to provide as an alternative to this bridge which is now closing off traffic to a major port on the lake at Bala Park.

ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REQUEST FOR RETENTION OF MUSICAL RIDE AND EQUESTRIAN DUTIES
speechtext:
My appearance here tonight arises through a misunderstanding. I had a consultation with Mr. Speaker about a question I had directed yesterday to the Solicitor General. I want to go on record that I have no criticism to make of the Speaker regarding the decision he reached. I apologize to him for having misunderstood him and gone through the motions I did to catch his eye, though perhaps I benefit-ted from it because I needed the exercise.
It is not my purpose to use my time debating with the Solicitor General about the problem I raised. There has been a change in the training of officers and men of the R.C.M.P. which has resulted in a curtailment in the use of horses. That is not the point at difference here. It is understood that the personnel, horses and necessary training equipment for the musical ride will be maintained for traditional and other purposes but, whether it is just a rumour or not, it is said that the training establishment is going to be moved to Ottawa.
DEBATES	October 6, 1966
This has caused great concern in my area and province, which for many years have been the centre for such training. We do not think there can be a good reason for moving the operation, and my purpose in asking the question of the Solicitor General was to establish precisely what the situation will be. So, without further debate I again ask him, is the government giving consideration to removing from the R.C.M.P. establishment in Regina the training equipment, forces and personnel needed for the musical ride and other equestrian duties? If so, has a final decision been taken, or is the minister giving sympathetic consideration to the many representations that these facilities should remain in Regina for historic and other substantial reasons?
